turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think it is very hard to be the right amount of AGI-pilled. It's very easy to build the product for the super AGI strong model. The hard thing is figuring out for the current model, how do you elicit the maximum capability?
turns.zh: 我觉得要做到「恰到好处的 AGI 信仰」非常难。为那个超强的 AGI 级模型去做产品很容易，难的是针对当前这个模型，怎么把它的能力最大限度地激发出来。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I've never seen anything like the pace folks at Anthropic are shipping at.
turns.zh: 我从没见过像 Anthropic 这样的上线速度。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: We want to remove every single barrier to shipping things. The timelines for a lot of our product features have gone down from six month to one month and sometimes to even one day.
turns.zh: 我们想把上线路上的每一道障碍都拆掉。我们很多产品功能的周期，已经从六个月缩短到一个月，有时甚至只要一天。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: You're interviewing hundreds of PMs and you just keep feeling like they're approaching it very incorrectly.
turns.zh: 你面试了几百位 PM，却总觉得他们的思路都不太对。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: The PM role is changing a lot. It's changing really quickly. The thing that is extremely important for building AI-native products is iterating so quickly, figuring out a way for you to actually launch features every single week.
turns.zh: PM 这个角色正在发生很大的变化，而且变得非常快。打造 AI 原生产品，极其重要的一点是迭代要足够快，想办法做到每周都能发布新功能。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What do you think are the emerging skills PMs need to develop?
turns.zh: 你觉得 PM 需要培养哪些新兴能力？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It comes back to product taste. As code becomes much cheaper to write, the thing that becomes more valuable is deciding what to write.
turns.zh: 归根结底还是产品品味。代码越来越便宜，越来越有价值的就是决定该写什么。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Cat, welcome to the podcast.
turns.zh: Cat，欢迎来到播客。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢邀请。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I have so many questions. I'm so excited to have you on this podcast. I want to start with giving people an understanding of your role alongside Boris. Everybody knows Boris. His episode is the number one most popular episode on this podcast, no pressure. He created Claude Code. He leads the eng team, ships a bazillion PRs a day from his phone, just like... I don't even know what the number is anymore. I think people don't give you enough credit for the success that Claude Code has had and Cowork and all the things you all are building. Help us understand your role on the team, how you work with Boris, how you split responsibilities. Just like what does the PMO look like on the Claude Code team?
turns.zh: 我有太多问题想问了，能请你来做客我特别兴奋。先请你给大家讲讲，你和 Boris 在角色上是怎么搭配的。大家都认识 Boris，他那一期是这个播客最受欢迎的一期，没压力哈。他创建了 Claude Code，带领工程团队，每天用手机提交海量 PR，我都不知道现在具体是多少了。我觉得大家对 Claude Code 和 Cowork 以及你们正在做的所有这些事情的成功，没有给你足够的功劳。请讲讲你在团队里的角色，你怎么和 Boris 配合，职责怎么分。Claude Code 团队的产品管理到底是什么样的？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I feel very lucky to work with Boris. He's been an amazing thought partner. He's our tech lead. He's very much the product visionary, and he is great at setting, "This is what the product needs to be in three months, six months from now. This is what the AGI-pilled version of the product is," and a lot of my role is figuring out, okay, what is the path from where we are today to that vision three to six months from now? And I spend more of my time on the cross-functional, so making sure that our marketing team, sales team, finance, capacity, et cetera, are bought in on the plan and that we're all rowing the same direction and that once the feature is ready, that there aren't any blockers to shipping it.
turns.zh: 我觉得自己非常幸运能和 Boris 共事。他是一位很棒的思考伙伴，是我们的技术负责人，也完全是产品的远见者。他特别擅长定下「三个月后、六个月后产品应该是什么样子」，「这就是这个产品 AGI 信仰版本的样子」。而我的工作很大一部分，是想清楚从今天的位置到三到六个月后的那个愿景，路径是什么。我花更多时间在跨部门协作上，确保市场团队、销售团队、财务、算力容量等等都认同这个计划，大家劲往一处使，并且功能一旦准备好，上线路上不会有任何阻碍。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think in many ways it works well because we kind of mind meld, but it is actually remarkably blurry of a line. I think we're 80% mind meld, and then there's this 20% of things that maybe I care a lot more about than Boris, so I'll drive those and 20% work he cares a lot more than me and he just drives those.
turns.zh: 我觉得很多方面这样运转得很好，是因为我们有点心有灵犀，但这条分界线其实出乎意料地模糊。大概 80% 是我们俩想法完全一致，剩下 20% 里，有些事我可能比 Boris 更在意，就由我来推动；另外 20% 是他比我更在意的，就由他来推动。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Something that you shared actually before we started recording is the fact that you're interviewing hundreds of PMs all the time. If I had a nickel every time someone asked me for an intro to someone at Anthropic to go work at Anthropic as a PM, I'd have 30 billion in ARR. It's just the number one place people want to go work at. So I can only imagine how many PMs you're interviewing. You told me that you're just seeing people doing it wrong, the way they're approaching what they think it takes to be a successful AIPM. Talk about what you're seeing and what people need to understand about what it takes to be successful these days.
turns.zh: 你在开始录制之前分享过一件事：你一直在面试几百位 PM。我要是每次有人找我介绍 Anthropic 的人、想去 Anthropic 当 PM，就能收一个五分镍币，我现在已经有 300 亿美元的 ARR 了。那里就是大家最想去的地方，所以我完全能想象你要面试多少 PM。你告诉我，你看到大家做得不对，也就是他们对「要成为一名成功的 AI PM 需要什么」的理解有偏差。讲讲你看到了什么，以及现在要成功，大家需要理解什么。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think before AI, technology shifts were a lot slower, so you could plan on these six to 12 month time horizons, and because you were shipping features at a bit of a slower rate, there was a lot more emphasis on coordinating with all the other partner teams to make sure that their shipping features that unblock your features because code at that time was very expensive to make. I think now with AI and with how much that has accelerated engineering and with how quickly the model capabilities are improving, the timelines for a lot of our product features have gone down from six month to one month and sometimes to one week or even one day. And with that, we actually need to make sure that products ship quite quickly.
turns.zh: 我觉得在 AI 之前，技术变迁要慢得多，所以你可以按六到十二个月的时间跨度做规划。而且因为你上线功能的节奏偏慢，会更强调和所有合作团队协调，确保他们上线的功能能为你的功能扫清障碍，因为那时候写代码是很昂贵的。现在有了 AI，工程效率大幅提升，模型能力又进步得这么快，我们很多产品功能的周期已经从六个月缩短到一个月，有时甚至缩短到一周乃至一天。这样一来，我们就必须保证产品能非常快地上线。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And what that means is as a PM, there should be less emphasis on making sure that you're aligning your multi-quarter roadmaps with your partner teams and more emphasis on, okay, how can we figure out the fastest way to get something out the door? How can we figure out how to make a concept corner of our product suite where we can just... An engineer has an idea or a PM has an idea, and by the end of the week, we are able to get into our user's hands. I think the PMs who do the best on AI-native products are the ones who can figure out, how can I shorten the time from having this idea to actually getting the product in the hands of users and help define what are the most important tasks that need to work out of the box for my product?
turns.zh: 这意味着，作为 PM，应该少花精力去把你的多季度路线图和合作团队对齐，多去想：怎样才能找到把东西推出去的最快办法？怎样才能划出产品线里的一小块地方，让工程师有了想法、或者 PM 有了想法，到周末就能送到用户手里？我觉得在 AI 原生产品上做得最好的 PM，都是在想：我怎么才能缩短从有想法到产品真正到用户手中的时间，并帮忙定义出对我的产品来说，哪些最重要的任务必须开箱即用？

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So what I love about this is what you're saying is just like people haven't grasped how fast they need to move and how much of the job now is helping the team move fast. What helps do that? What do you do, what does your PM team do to help them move this fast other than have access to the most advanced models?
turns.zh: 我喜欢你这个说法的地方在于：大家还没意识到自己需要多快，也没意识到现在这份工作很大一部分是帮助团队更快地行动。那有什么能帮上忙？除了能用上最先进的模型之外，你和你的 PM 团队还做了什么，来帮大家跑得这么快？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think the first thing is to set clear goals. Because LLMs are so general, that actually creates a lot of ambiguity in who we're building for, what problems we're trying to solve, what the top use cases are. And so I think a great PM is able to say, "Okay, our key user is professional developers. The main problem that we want to solve for this feature is maybe there's too many permission prompts and people are feeling fatigue, and the use case is we want professional developers at enterprises to safely get to zero permission prompts." And that actually sets a pretty clear goal because it rules out a lot of potential approaches for reducing permission prompts so that people can get a lot more done with one prompt.
turns.zh: 我觉得第一件事是设定清晰的目标。因为大语言模型太通用了，这反而会让我们到底为谁做、要解决什么问题、最主要的用例是什么，变得含糊不清。所以一个优秀的 PM 能够说：「我们的核心用户是专业开发者。这个功能要解决的主要问题，可能是权限提示太多，大家觉得疲劳；用例是让企业里的专业开发者能安全地做到零权限提示。」这就设定了一个相当清晰的目标，因为它排除了很多减少权限提示的可行做法，让大家用一次提示词就能多做很多事。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And then I think the second thing that's very important is figuring out some repeatable process for getting these features shipped. So for Claude Code, what we do is we actually ship almost all of our features in research preview. We clearly brand this when we ship something so that users know that this is an early product, this is just an idea, this is just something that we're trying to get feedback on and iterating on, and that this might not be supported forever. And what this does is it reduces our commitment for shipping something. We can just get something out in a week or two.
turns.zh: 第二件非常重要的事，是找到一套可重复的流程，把这些功能上线。对 Claude Code 来说，我们几乎所有功能都以研究预览的形式发布。上线时我们会清楚地标明，让用户知道这是早期产品，只是一个想法，是我们想拿来收集反馈、继续迭代的东西，而且可能不会一直支持下去。这样做降低了我们发布一个东西所要承担的承诺，我们一两周就能把东西推出去。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And then the third thing that a PM should do is help create the framework for the team so that they know when to pull in cross-functional partners and what those cross-functional partners' expectations are. So for example, we have a really tight process between engineering, marketing, and docs. So when engineers have a feature that they feel is ready and that we've dogfooded internally, they post it in our evergreen launch room, and then Sarah, who leads our docs, and Alex who leads PMM, Antaric and Lydia on DevRel just jump in and can turn around the marketing announcement for it the very next day. And because we have this really tight process, it lowers the friction for any engineer to ship something, and PM is the role that should be setting this up.
turns.zh: 第三件事，PM 应该帮团队建立一套框架，让大家知道什么时候该拉跨部门的伙伴进来，以及这些伙伴有什么期望。比如，我们在工程、市场和文档之间有一套非常紧密的流程。当工程师觉得某个功能已经就绪、而且我们内部已经自用过了，就会发到我们长期开放的发布群里，然后负责文档的 Sarah、负责产品营销的 Alex，还有负责开发者关系的 Antaric 和 Lydia 就会立刻跟进，第二天就能出来营销发布内容。有了这套很紧密的流程，任何工程师上线东西的阻力都变小了，而搭建这套流程正是 PM 该做的。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How do PRDs fit into this and the fact that you said that goals are a really important part, just like being aligned on what does success look like? Who is this for? Who's this now for? Are you writing PRDs, is it just a couple bullet points? How's that evolved in the world of a PM?
turns.zh: 那 PRD 在这里面怎么放？你说目标是很重要的一环，就是对齐成功是什么样子，这是给谁用的，又是给谁用的？你们写 PRD 吗，还是只有几条要点？在 PM 的世界里这件事是怎么演变的？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So there's two things that we do. One is we have very rigorous metrics and we do metrics readouts with the entire team every week. The goal of this is to make sure that everyone deeply understands all the facets of our business, what our key goals are, how they're trending, and what drives them. The second thing that we do is we have this list of team principles, and this includes who our key users are, why those are our key users, and the reason that we articulate all of this is so that everybody on the team feels like they understand how our business works, they understand what's important to us and what we're willing to trade off, and it lets people make decisions by themselves without feeling like they're blocked on PM or any other stakeholder.
turns.zh: 我们做两件事。第一，我们有非常严格的指标，每周都会和整个团队一起做指标复盘。目的是让每个人都深入理解我们业务的方方面面：关键目标是什么，趋势如何，是什么在驱动它们。第二，我们有一份团队原则清单，里面包括我们的核心用户是谁，为什么是他们。我们把这些都明确写下来，是为了让团队里每个人都觉得自己理解我们的业务是怎么运转的，理解对我们来说什么重要、我们愿意做什么取舍，这样大家就能自己做决定，不会觉得被卡在 PM 或其他相关方那里。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I love how so much of this is like, okay, we still need PMs in the future, and there's so much talk of why do we need PMs? We're just going to ship and build. We need engineers.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢这里面的很多观点，就是说，我们将来还是需要 PM 的。现在有很多说法，说为什么要 PM？我们直接上线、直接做就行了，我们需要的是工程师。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Oh, we actually do PRDs sometimes. So I think for features that are particularly ambiguous, it does help to write out just a one-pager on what the goals are, what the delightful use cases are, what the failure modes currently are that we need to fix. And there are occasionally some projects, especially things that require heavy infrastructure that do take many months, and for those situations, we do write PRDs still.
turns.zh: 哦，我们有时候其实也会写 PRD。对于特别模糊的功能，写一页纸说明目标是什么、哪些用例会让人惊喜、目前有哪些需要修复的失败情形，确实有帮助。还有一些项目，尤其是需要大量基础设施的，要花好几个月，这种情况下我们依然会写 PRD。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I want to drill a little bit further into just how you're able to move so fast. I've never seen anything like the pace folks at Anthropic are shipping at. Someone made this calendar of launches across Anthropic, and it was literally every day there was a major feature or product. So one question people had online is you guys just launched this, not launched, but built this incredible model Mythos that is still in preview because it's so powerful, people are a little afraid of what it can do. Have you guys been using this? Is this part of the reason you've been able to move so fast?
turns.zh: 我想再深入问问你们怎么能走得这么快。我从没见过像 Anthropic 这样的上线速度。有人做了一份 Anthropic 全公司的发布日历，真的是每天都有重大功能或产品。网上有人提出一个问题：你们刚刚发布，不对，是做出了这个了不起的模型 Mythos，它因为太强大还停留在预览阶段，大家有点担心它能做什么。你们有在用吗？这是你们能走这么快的原因之一吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: We've been moving pretty fast for several quarters now, so I think it's not fully Mythos. Mythos is an incredibly powerful model. We do use the models internally, and I think this has increased our rate of shipping a little bit, but I don't think it explains the bulk of the increase. I think a lot of it is the process and the expectation on the team. So we're very low on process. We want to remove every single barrier to shipping things. We want to make sure every single person on the team feels empowered to take their idea from just an idea to out in the world in less than a week, sometimes even in a day.
turns.zh: 我们已经连续好几个季度保持很快的节奏了，所以我觉得不全是因为 Mythos。Mythos 是一个非常强大的模型。我们确实会在内部使用这些模型，这在一定程度上提高了我们的上线速度，但我不认为它能解释大部分的提升。我觉得很大程度上是流程，以及团队里的预期。我们的流程非常少。我们想把上线路上每一道障碍都拆掉。我们想确保团队里每个人都有底气，把自己的想法从一个念头变成上线到外面的东西，用不了一周，有时甚至一天。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Cool. Oh, man. What an advantage to have the best model and also be building product. That's so cool.
turns.zh: 太棒了。天哪，既拥有最好的模型，同时又在做产品，这是多大的优势啊。太酷了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: We are very lucky to be able to work with the frontier models.
turns.zh: 我们非常幸运，能和前沿模型一起工作。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Oh my God, what an awesome advantage, just build a thing and then use it and then accelerate faster. It's so interesting. There's a couple of these other side things, I want to just go on these sidequest on this conversation. There's so much happening with Anthropic, and I just am so curious to get your insight. One is a week ago or so, the whole source code of Claude Code leaked. Somebody got it out there. I think it was a mistake someone made. Is there anything you comment there, just like what happened? What went wrong? What should people know?
turns.zh: 天哪，这优势太惊人了，做个东西，然后自己用，再加速前进。太有意思了。我还想顺便聊几个旁支话题，借这个机会问问。Anthropic 最近有太多事情，我特别想听听你的看法。其一，大概一周前，Claude Code 的完整源代码泄露了，有人把它弄到了网上。我想是某个人的失误。你有什么可以评论的吗？到底发生了什么，哪里出了问题？大家应该知道些什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So we immediately looked into this when we saw it. We realized that this was the result of human error. There was a human working with Claude to write PR. This was just an update to how we release our packages and it actually went through two layers of human review, and so this was a result of human error and we've hardened our processes to make sure that it doesn't happen in the future.
turns.zh: 我们看到之后立刻着手调查了。我们确认这是人为失误导致的。当时有一个人在和 Claude 一起写一个 PR，那只是对我们发布软件包的方式做的一次更新，它其实还经过了两层人工审核，所以这是人为失误的结果，我们已经加固了流程，确保将来不会再发生。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Is this person still at Anthropic? Are they doing all right?
turns.zh: 那个人还在 Anthropic 吗？他还好吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yes, yes. It's a process failure, and the most important thing is to just learn from it and to add more safeguards so that doesn't happen again, and so that's what we've been focused on and most of those have shifted.
turns.zh: 在的，在的。这是流程上的失误，最重要的是从中吸取教训，增加更多保障措施，避免再次发生，这就是我们一直在专注做的，而且大部分措施已经落实了。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Okay. Another question I had is OpenClaw. So recently there's been this move to keep people from using Claude's subscription with their OpenClaws. People got really upset. They're confused why this is happening. It feels like there's harm caused to the open source community. What do people need to understand about what went into this decision?
turns.zh: 好的。我的另一个问题是 OpenClaw。最近有一个动作，不让大家用 Claude 的订阅来跑他们的 OpenClaw。大家非常不满，也很困惑为什么会这样。感觉这对开源社区造成了伤害。大家需要了解，这个决定背后有哪些考量？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So we've been seeing a lot of demand for Claude, and we've been working very hard to both scale our infrastructure and also to make our harness more token efficient so that you can get more usage out of it. It wasn't designed for third-party products, which have different usage patterns than our first-party ones. We spent a bunch of time trying to figure out what is the most seamless transition that we can offer, and so I was very happy to be able to say that everyone gets some credits alongside their subscription. But yeah, we did have to make the hard decision that we needed to prioritize our first-party products and our API, and so this is the decision that resulted from that.
turns.zh: 我们看到对 Claude 的需求非常旺盛，我们一直在努力扩展基础设施，也在让我们的运行框架更省 token，这样你就能用得更久。它当初并不是为第三方产品设计的，而第三方产品的使用模式和我们自家产品不一样。我们花了很多时间，想弄清楚我们能提供的最平滑的过渡方案是什么，所以我很高兴能宣布，每个人在订阅之外都会获得一些额度。不过，是的，我们确实不得不做出艰难的决定：必须优先保障我们自家的产品和 API，这就是由此产生的决定。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Yeah. To me, it makes so much sense. You guys are subsidizing this usage at 200 bucks a month and it's basically unlimited use of this. And I think people don't understand. Businesses are trying to make money. We're trying to be profitable here. We can't just give away compute when it's so in demand. So I get it. Coming back to the PM team, what does just the PM team look like at Anthropic? How many PMs are there? How are they kind of organized?
turns.zh: 是的。对我来说这完全说得通。你们每个月 200 美元，基本上是无限量使用，等于在补贴这些用量。我觉得大家没理解这一点。企业是要赚钱的，我们要盈利。算力需求这么大，我们不能白送算力。所以我理解。回到 PM 团队的话题，Anthropic 的 PM 团队到底是什么样的？有多少 PM？大致是怎么组织的？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, so we have a few PM teams. I think we're maybe around 30 or 40 PMs right now. So we have the research PM team who Diane leads, and this team is responsible for understanding all of the feedback from our customers for our models, and then feeding that to the best research team to act on it, and they also shepherd the model launch. There's the Claude developer platform team that maintains the APIs that Claude Code is built on top of, and they also release things like Managed Agents, which is a way for you to build your agents and we can host it on your behalf. And then there's Claude Code that works on both Claude Code and the Cowork core products.
turns.zh: 是的，我们有几个 PM 团队。我想现在大概有 30 到 40 位 PM。有研究 PM 团队，由 Diane 带领，这个团队负责了解客户对我们模型的所有反馈，然后把这些反馈交给最合适的研究团队去处理，他们也负责推动模型发布。还有 Claude 开发者平台团队，负责维护 Claude Code 所构建于其上的那些 API，他们也发布 Managed Agents 这类东西，也就是你来构建自己的智能体，由我们替你托管。然后还有 Claude Code 团队，同时负责 Claude Code 和 Cowork 这两个核心产品。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: There's enterprise that helps make Claude Code and Cowork easier to adopt for all of our enterprise customers, and so this is everything from cost controls, our back security controls, and just making sure that these enterprises feel very confident and comfortable using our tools. And then we also have our growth team that is responsible for growing across our entire product suite. So we work very closely with them on Claude Code and Cowork growth. And I know they also work with our other teams on CDP growth, so growth of people who use the Claude API.
turns.zh: 还有企业团队，帮助我们所有企业客户更容易地采用 Claude Code 和 Cowork，从成本控制、基于角色的访问控制（RBAC）、安全控制，到确保这些企业用我们的工具时感到非常有信心、很放心。此外我们还有增长团队，负责整个产品线的增长。我们在 Claude Code 和 Cowork 的增长上和他们合作非常紧密。我知道他们也和我们其他团队合作 CDP 增长，也就是使用 Claude API 的人群的增长。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So speaking of growth, so Amol was just on the podcast. You have this really interesting insight that most people haven't been sharing. There's always this sense that we need fewer PMs in the future. Why do we need PMs? Engineers can do ship. His take is that because engineers are moving so fast, PMs and designers are squeezed. There's less time to stay on top of everything that is happening. There's a feature shipping every day. So his take is he needs more PMs because it's hard to keep up. What's your take there? Do you feel like there'll be an increase in hiring of PMs? What do you think is going on with the PM profession long-term?
turns.zh: 说到增长，Amol 刚刚上过这个播客。他有一个很有意思的洞见，是大多数人没有分享过的。大家总觉得未来需要的 PM 会更少。为什么需要 PM？工程师自己就能上线。他的看法是，因为工程师动得太快，PM 和设计师被挤压了，没有足够的时间跟上所有正在发生的事情。每天都有功能上线。所以他的观点是他需要更多 PM，因为实在跟不上。你怎么看？你觉得 PM 的招聘会增加吗？你觉得 PM 这个职业长期会怎么发展？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think all of the roles are merging. PMs are doing some engineering work, engineers are doing PM work, designers are PMing and also landing code. You can either hire a lot more engineers who have great product taste, or you can keep your engineering hiring the same and hire a lot more PMs to help guide some of their work. On our team, we're pretty focused on hiring engineers with great product taste. This way, we can reduce the amount of overhead for shipping any product. There are many engineers on our team who are fully able to end to end go from see user feedback on Twitter through to ship a product at the end of the week with almost no product involvement. And this I think is actually the most efficient way to ship something.
turns.zh: 我觉得所有角色都在融合。PM 在做一些工程工作，工程师在做 PM 的工作，设计师在做 PM 的事，同时也在提交代码。你可以多招很多有出色产品品味的工程师，也可以保持工程招聘不变，多招很多 PM 来帮忙引导他们的工作。在我们团队，我们比较专注于招有出色产品品味的工程师。这样我们能减少任何产品上线的协调开销。我们团队有不少工程师完全有能力端到端地完成：从在 Twitter 上看到用户反馈，到周末前把产品上线，几乎不需要产品团队介入。我认为这其实是上线东西最高效的方式。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So I think engineer and PM are kind of overlapping and you will get a lot of benefit from having more of either. I think product taste is still a very rare skill to have, and we'll pretty much hire anyone who we feel has demonstrated this strongly.
turns.zh: 所以我觉得工程和 PM 在某种程度上是重叠的，不管多招哪一边，你都会获益良多。我觉得产品品味依然是一种非常稀缺的能力，只要我们觉得谁清楚地证明了自己有这种能力，我们基本上都会招。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And your background was in engineering, right?
turns.zh: 你的背景是工程，对吧？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, I was an engineer for many years. I was then a VC very briefly before joining Anthropic, and actually almost all the PMs on our team have either been engineers or ship code here on Claude Code, and so that's one of the things that I think helps build trust with the team and also just enables us to move a lot faster. And then actually our designers also have been front end engineers before.
turns.zh: 对，我做了很多年工程师。在加入 Anthropic 之前，我短暂地做过一阵 VC。其实我们团队几乎所有 PM 要么做过工程师，要么在 Claude Code 这里自己提交代码，我觉得这是帮助赢得团队信任的因素之一，也让我们能走得快得多。另外我们的设计师以前也都做过前端工程师。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Wow. Because that's the big question, there's definitely this emerging that's happening, the Venn diagrams are combining. I think the big question for a lot of people is if you're coming from engineering or product or design, which of those core skills is going to be most valuable? I could see it Anthropic and on Claude Code, engineering is very valuable. I'm curious if other companies, if you have a design background becoming a PM is more valuable or just a PM-PM.
turns.zh: 哇。因为这正是大家最关心的问题，现在确实有一种趋势，几个角色的韦恩图在重叠。我想很多人的疑问是：如果你出身工程、产品或者设计，这几种核心能力里哪一种会最有价值？我能想象在 Anthropic、在 Claude Code 上，工程能力非常有价值。我好奇的是，在其他公司，如果你有设计背景，转做 PM 是不是更有价值，还是说纯粹的 PM 更吃香。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I still think it comes back to product taste. As code becomes much cheaper to write, the thing that becomes more valuable is deciding what to write. What is the right UX for this feature? What is the most delightful way that a user can experience it? We get tens of thousands of GitHub issues asking for every single thing under the sun, and it takes a lot of care and taste to figure out, okay, which of these is worth building and what is the right way to build it? And I think that skillset can come from any background, but I think that's the most important thing.
turns.zh: 我仍然觉得最终还是回到产品品味。代码写起来越来越便宜，真正变得更有价值的是决定写什么。这个功能该是什么样的 UX？用户用起来怎样才最愉悦？我们收到成千上万条 GitHub issue，什么需求都有，要从里面判断哪些值得做、又该怎么做，需要很用心，也需要品味。我觉得这种能力可以来自任何背景，但它是最重要的。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think the reason why an engineering background is particularly useful, at least for the next few months, is if you have an engineering background, you have a better sense for how hard something should be, and that's often a factor in what you choose to build. So if something is very easy to build, then maybe instead of debating it, you just spend an hour doing it, but if something is harder to build and you know that upfront, then you know that, okay, this will just cost a lot more for our team to get this out the door. So it helps a bit with the prioritization.
turns.zh: 至少在接下来的几个月里，工程背景之所以特别有用，是因为你对一件事应该有多难有更好的判断，而这往往是决定做什么的一个因素。如果某件事很容易做，那也许不用争论，花一个小时直接做出来就行；但如果某件事更难做，而你一开始就知道，那你就清楚这会让团队付出多得多的成本才能上线。所以它对排优先级有一些帮助。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: You said for the next few months, is that just because the models will get so good potentially in the next few months, you may not even need to know that as much?
turns.zh: 你说「接下来的几个月」，是因为模型可能在未来几个月里变得非常强，到时候你甚至不太需要懂这些了吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think the valued skillsets does change quite frequently, and so it's really hard to predict more than a few months out. So it's less a commentary on what shift I think will happen and more of a commentary that I think large shifts will happen.
turns.zh: 我觉得哪些技能有价值，变化得相当频繁，所以很难预测几个月以后的事。所以这与其说是在评论具体会发生什么转变，不如说是在说：我认为会发生巨大的转变。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So you're not saying that's when Mythos comes out and will change everything and that we don't need to know anything about engineering?
turns.zh: 所以你不是在说，等 Mythos 发布、一切都被改变之后，我们就完全不需要懂工程了？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: No, I'm just saying that every few months it seems like there's a large increase in coding capability, which then changes what other roles are valuable. I think the most important thing is to be able to have this first principles thinking where you can figure out how the tech landscape is changing, what the team really needs from you, and to jump in and fix that hole because I think the work is becoming more amorphous, which means that a great PM is able to understand what all the gaps are to figure out what the highest priority ones are, and then to just figure out, okay, how do I learn that skillset or what is the skillset that I have that I can apply to this challenge? So I think the current environment values people who are able to wear a lot of hats, are able to swap them, and are very low ego about what work they do to help the team move faster.
turns.zh: 不是，我的意思只是，每隔几个月，编码能力似乎就会大幅提升，进而改变其他角色的价值所在。我觉得最重要的是具备第一性原理的思考方式：能弄清楚技术格局在怎么变化、团队真正需要你做什么，然后跳进去把这个缺口补上。因为工作正变得越来越不成形，这意味着一个优秀的 PM 要能看清所有的缺口，判断哪些优先级最高，然后想清楚：我该怎么学会这项技能，或者我已有的哪项技能可以用来应对这个挑战。所以我觉得当下的环境看重的是这样的人：能身兼多职、能随时切换角色，而且在做什么工作上毫无架子，只想帮团队跑得更快。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I love this answer. There's this question I've been asking people in your shoes, folks that are kind of at the bleeding edge of what AI is capable of and building with the latest tools, which is just where will human brains continue to be useful and necessary for a while until we get to super intelligence. What I'm hearing here is essentially picking the things to work on, knowing where the market's going and figuring out what to prioritize essentially, and then it's knowing if the thing you've built is good and right and getting it out there in some early version at least. Does that sound right? Is there anything else of just where human brains will continue to be useful for at least the next few months?
turns.zh: 我喜欢这个回答。我一直在问身处你这种位置的人一个问题，就是你们站在 AI 能力的最前沿，用着最新的工具在做东西，那么在我们抵达超级智能之前，人类的大脑在哪些方面仍会持续有用、不可或缺？我听下来，大致是：挑选要做的事，知道市场走向、搞清楚该优先做什么，然后判断自己做出来的东西好不好、对不对，并且至少先以某个早期版本推出去。这样说对吗？至少在接下来的几个月里，人类的大脑还有哪些地方会继续有用，还有别的吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think humans still provide a level of common sense that the models don't, and there's a thousand moving pieces to any product launch, some of them are very small, but there's always a lot that could potentially go wrong. I think the model doesn't always have a great sense of who all the stakeholders are, how they relate to each other, what their preferences are, what are the right venues to communicate with them, to keep them on board. I think a lot of this more tacit common sense EQ kind of knowledge is still very valuable. Of course, we want the models to get better at this and I think they will be, but right now I think there's still gaps.
turns.zh: 我觉得人类仍然提供着一种模型所没有的常识。任何一次产品发布都有上千个活动的部件，有些很小，但总有很多地方可能出岔子。模型并不总能清楚地知道谁是所有的利益相关方、他们之间是什么关系、各自的偏好是什么、该通过什么渠道跟他们沟通、怎样让他们一直支持你。我觉得这类更偏隐性的常识和情商方面的知识，依然非常有价值。当然，我们希望模型在这方面变得更好，我认为它们会的，但现在还是有差距。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How do you just deal as a human going through so much constant change, just being on the inside of the tornado, maybe it's calm there, but just like how do you stay on top of what's going on? How do you stay sane through all this craziness that we're moving through?
turns.zh: 作为一个人，你要怎么应对这么多持续不断的变化？你身处龙卷风的中心，也许那里是平静的，但你怎么跟上正在发生的一切？在这一切疯狂之中，你怎么保持理智？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think our team is still people who lean into the chaos. So we try to face every challenge with a smile because there's always so much going on. There's always so many risks and tricky situations that if you get too stressed about anything, you'll burn out, and so we really look for people who can kind of look at a challenge, be like, "Whew, that's going to be hard, but I'm excited to tackle it and I'm going to do the best that I possibly can. And I know I won't be perfect, but I'll be able to sleep at night knowing that I did my best."
turns.zh: 我觉得我们团队仍然是一群拥抱混乱的人。所以我们尽量笑着面对每一个挑战，因为事情实在太多了，风险和棘手的情况也太多了，如果你对任何一件事过于焦虑，就会被耗尽。所以我们特别想找的是这样的人：看着一个挑战，会说「哎呀，这会很难，但我很期待去解决它，我会尽我所能做到最好。我知道自己不会完美，但想到我已经尽力了，我晚上就能睡得着。」

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: That's an interesting answer to just what skills will be important in this future because it's... I forget who said this, maybe Ben Mann, that this is the most normal the world will ever be.
turns.zh: 对于「未来什么能力重要」，这是个有意思的回答，因为……我忘了是谁说的了，可能是 Ben Mann，说现在是世界有史以来最正常的时候了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, it definitely gets harder. I feel like there are a lot of weeks where maybe Sunday night there's some P0 and then by Monday there's a P00 and by Monday afternoon there's a P000 and you're like, "Wow. I can't believe I was so worried about that P0 from Sunday." But I think you just have to acknowledge that there's only so much that you can do that you need to sleep well so that you can make good decisions next day and just brutally prioritize where you spend your time, what's the most important thing to get right and be okay letting things go. There's products that we ship that aren't as polished as I wish they were, but our top goal is to help empower professional developers, and if a product isn't successful, as long as it's not blocking the core use case, it's okay because we'll hear the feedback and we'll fix it in the next release.
turns.zh: 是的，确实越来越难。我感觉很多周都是这样：周日晚上出了个 P0，到周一又来了个 P00，周一下午又冒出个 P000，然后你会想：「哇，我居然曾经为周日那个 P0 那么担心。」但我觉得你只能承认，你能做的就这么多，你需要睡好觉，这样第二天才能做出好的决定，同时要毫不留情地排优先级：把时间花在哪里、最重要的是把什么事做对，并且接受放手一些事情。我们上线的产品里，有些没有我希望的那么精致，但我们的首要目标是赋能专业开发者，如果某个产品不太成功，只要它没有阻碍核心使用场景，就没关系，因为我们会听到反馈，在下一个版本里修好它。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Launching a feature that is buggy is the kind of thing that would have kept me up at night, but it is something that I'm now able to live with knowing that, okay, we're going to get that quick feedback and we're going to fix it in the next release.
turns.zh: 发布一个有 bug 的功能，以前是会让我夜不能寐的事，但现在我能接受了，因为我知道我们很快会得到反馈，然后在下一个版本里修复。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What I'm imagining is there's that GIF. I think it's maybe from Pirates of the Caribbean where it's this guy walking down a pair of stairs on a ship and the whole ship is just being demolished around him and he's so chill, just strolling down the staircases as everything's falling apart. And that's interesting because everyone I've met from Anthropic is just so chill and just so optimistic. Yeah, I think that's a really interesting insight is just like having this calmness and optimism versus just like, "Oh my God, everything's crazy and going nuts."
turns.zh: 我脑子里浮现的是那张 GIF，我想是《加勒比海盗》里的，一个人走下船上的楼梯，周围整艘船都在被摧毁，而他却悠然自得，一步步走下楼梯，眼看着一切分崩离析。这挺有意思的，因为我遇到的每个 Anthropic 的人都那么淡定、那么乐观。是的，我觉得这是个很有意思的洞察：保持这种平静和乐观，而不是「天哪，一切都疯了、乱套了」。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, I think if you don't have it, you'll get pretty burnt out. I think we also tend to hire people who have been in the industry for a while and have experienced lots of ups and downs and have a good sense for what gives them energy and how to maintain their energy over time, and I think that's helped us a lot.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得如果没有这种心态，你会相当倦怠。我们也倾向于招那些在行业里待了很久、经历过大起大落的人，他们很清楚什么能给自己带来能量，也知道怎么长期保持能量，我觉得这对我们帮助很大。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So interesting. Something that I wanted to ask about is, so there's these roles blurring, engineers are becoming PMs, everyone's dogs are cats, everyone's everyone. What do we lose in that world? Do we lose career ladders and clear career paths? Do we lose design consistency, code quality? There's probably some downsides. What are some things you find are just like, okay, that's something we're sacrificing for the greater good?
turns.zh: 太有意思了。我还想问一件事：现在角色的边界在变模糊，工程师在变成 PM，大家都在跨界，人人都能干所有人的活。在这样的世界里，我们失去了什么？我们会失去职业阶梯和清晰的职业路径吗？会失去设计的一致性、代码质量吗？大概会有一些负面影响。你觉得有哪些东西是我们为了更大的利益而牺牲掉的？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: We're sacrificing product consistency. Historically, when code was expensive to write, you would carefully plan out everything in your product suite, how every product relates to each other, what the use case for every single one is, how they integrate, and you would pretty much have one product for each use case, and now with AI moving so quickly and with so many ideas that we need to test out, we do sometimes have features that overlap with each other. A lot of the times it's because there's two form factors that we love internally and we want the external audience to tell us which one is better. What that means for someone who's a new user though is a new user might not know, okay, what is the best path to accomplish X? There is more education we need to do to help people understand what the core features are and what the best practices are for using them.
turns.zh: 我们牺牲的是产品的一致性。过去代码写起来很贵，你会仔细规划整个产品矩阵里的一切：每个产品之间是什么关系、每个产品对应什么使用场景、它们怎么整合，基本上每个使用场景只有一个产品。而现在，AI 发展得这么快，又有这么多想法需要测试，我们确实会有一些功能彼此重叠。很多时候，是因为内部有两种我们都很喜欢的形态，想让外部用户告诉我们哪一种更好。但这对新用户意味着，他可能不知道要完成 X，最好的路径是什么。我们需要做更多的教育，帮助大家理解哪些是核心功能，以及使用它们的最佳实践是什么。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think this is the cost of launching a lot of features. I think users also feel like it's hard to keep up with the latest. Usually in traditional PM, you ship a feature every month or quarter, and so it's really easy for a user to understand, okay, I just need to check in on this once a month and I'll learn some new things, and if I ignore it for six months, it's fine, I don't feel like I'm missing out. I think with these agentic tools, not just Claude Code and Cowork, but across the whole ecosystem, people feel this need to check Twitter every single day to see what the absolute latest thing is, and I think there's more we can do to help people feel less like they're on this ever increasingly fast treadmill and that they feel like... I would love people to feel like they can just open these tools, the tools will educate them or teach them what they want to know, and that they can just feel more bought along.
turns.zh: 我觉得这是推出大量功能的代价。我想用户也会觉得很难跟上最新进展。传统的产品管理里，你每个月或每个季度上线一个功能，用户很容易理解：我每月看一次就行，会学到一些新东西；就算半年不管，也没关系，不会觉得自己错过了什么。而有了这些智能体工具，不只是 Claude Code 和 Cowork，而是整个生态都是这样，大家觉得每天都得刷 Twitter，看看最新的东西到底是什么。我觉得我们可以多做些事，让大家不再觉得自己踩在一台越转越快的跑步机上，而是觉得……我希望大家可以直接打开这些工具，由工具来教会他们想知道的东西，让他们更有跟上节奏的感觉。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Yeah. I saw you launch this really interesting feature the other day. I think it's /powerup where it basically walks you through all the cool ways and basically all the best practices to use Claude Code. Is that kind of along these lines?
turns.zh: 对。我前几天看到你们上线了一个很有意思的功能，好像是 /powerup，它会带你过一遍使用 Claude Code 的各种酷炫玩法和最佳实践。是沿着这个思路吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, exactly. So in the past, we didn't actually want to do something like powerup, because we felt like the product should be intuitive enough that you don't actually need to go through any tutorial, and over time, we've just realized that there's just so many features and there's so much demand for a built-in onboarding experience that we diverged a bit from our original principle saying no onboarding flow and added this because there's just so many users who wanted to know there's a hundred features, what are the 10 that I absolutely need to use? And so we put that together.
turns.zh: 对，没错。以前我们其实不想做 powerup 这样的东西，因为我们觉得产品应该足够直观，你不需要走任何教程。但随着时间推移，我们发现功能实在太多了，大家对内置的上手引导需求也非常大，所以我们稍微背离了「不做引导流程」的原始原则，加了这个功能。因为有太多用户想知道：这里有上百个功能，我最需要用的那 10 个是什么？所以我们就把它做出来了。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Yeah, it's such a bizarre world. So Anthropic has been really successful with B2B enterprises where traditionally you don't launch a bunch of stuff, you just kind of have quarterly release maybe, and it's like the opposite of every day we got some new... So just maybe following that thread, the run Anthropic has been on as just otherworldly. Anthropic was way behind when it started. It was, Amol shared this, just like one of the least funded companies, didn't have distribution, wasn't the first to go, OpenAI was way ahead and it was just like no way Anthropic has any chance to compete significantly long-term. Now it's just killing it, just beating the biggest companies, teams. So much just like the growth is just... $11 billion in ARR in one month growth. By the time this comes out, it'd probably be even higher. Just being on the inside, what are some ingredients that have allowed Anthropic to be this successful and kind of come from behind and do this well?
turns.zh: 是啊，这个世界真奇妙。Anthropic 在 B2B 企业市场做得非常成功，而传统上在这个领域你不会推出一大堆东西，顶多按季度发布，而你们是完全相反，每天都有新东西。顺着这个话头聊，Anthropic 这一路的势头简直不可思议。Anthropic 起步时远远落后，Amol 分享过，它是资金最少的公司之一，没有分销渠道，也不是第一个入场的，OpenAI 遥遥领先，当时大家觉得 Anthropic 没有任何机会能长期有意义地竞争。现在它却势如破竹，把最大的公司和团队都甩在身后。增长太惊人了，一个月就增加 110 亿美元的 ARR。等这期播出的时候，可能数字还会更高。从内部来看，有哪些要素让 Anthropic 能够这样成功，从落后一路追上来，而且做得这么好？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: The two most important things are, one, this unifying mission. It's hard to state how important this is. We hire people who care most about bringing safe AGI to all of humanity, and this is actually something that we reference frequently in our decisions about what our entire product org should focus on shipping. And because we put this mission above any individual product line, we're able to make Make very fast decisions that cut across the entire org and execute on them in a unified way. So I think this is something that I've never seen at a company of our scale.
turns.zh: 最重要的有两点，第一，是统一的使命。这一点的重要性怎么强调都不为过。我们招的是最在乎把安全的 AGI 带给全人类的人，而且我们在决定整个产品组织应该专注上线什么时，也经常拿它作为参照。因为我们把这个使命放在任何单一产品线之上，所以能做出跨整个组织的快速决策，并且统一地执行。我在这么大规模的公司里从没见过这样的情况。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And so just to make sure that's clear, so essentially having the number one mission is safety, alignment, making sure AI is good for the world, and you're saying just having that as a clear mission makes decisions a lot easier to make.
turns.zh: 我确认一下我理解对了：本质上就是，第一使命是安全、对齐，确保 AI 对世界是好的，而你是说，把这一点作为清晰的使命，会让做决策容易很多。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: If there's two competing priorities, we'll talk about which one is more important for Anthropic's mission, and it makes it a lot easier to decide which of the two we prioritize and then everyone will stand behind the one that we decide. And so sometimes that means that, hey, we want to ship something on Claude Code, but this other thing is more important, and so we deprioritize shipping this and we just wait until later.
turns.zh: 如果有两个优先级相互冲突，我们会讨论哪一个对 Anthropic 的使命更重要，这样就容易得多地决定优先哪一个，然后所有人都会支持这个决定。所以有时候这意味着，我们本来想在 Claude Code 上上线某个东西，但另一件事更重要，于是我们就把它往后放，等以后再上线。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What's really interesting about that is that explains, I think, versus another company maybe rhymes with OpenAI did a lot of different things, and what I'm hearing here essentially is like, okay, we're not going to launch a social network, we're not going to launch a feed of interesting information because it's not aligned to this mission, and that has kept Anthropic focused, which seems to be a core ingredient to the success.
turns.zh: 这一点很有意思，我觉得它解释了为什么和另一家名字有点像 OpenAI 的公司不同，那家公司做了很多不同的事情。而我听到的是，我们不会去做社交网络，不会去做一个信息流，因为这不符合使命，这让 Anthropic 保持专注，而专注似乎是成功的核心要素之一。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Well, when I think about mission, I think about putting Anthropic's goals ahead of any individual org or any individual product. And so for me, it's... I think the second thing that we're very good at is focus. I think mission to me is slightly different. Mission means that teams are willing to make sacrifices that hurt their own goals and their own KRs in service of Anthropic's goals and Anthropic's KRs, and people are very happy to make those trade-offs. So an extreme example is if Claude Code failed, but Anthropic succeeded, I would be extremely happy. And the whole team is very willing to make decisions that follow that chain of thought.
turns.zh: 嗯，我说到使命，指的是把 Anthropic 的目标置于任何单个组织、单个产品之上。所以对我来说……我觉得我们第二个非常擅长的是专注。在我看来使命稍有不同。使命意味着，团队愿意为了 Anthropic 的目标和 Anthropic 的 KR 做出牺牲，哪怕这会损害自己团队的目标和 KR，而且大家都很乐意做这样的取舍。举个极端的例子，如果 Claude Code 失败了，但 Anthropic 成功了，我会非常开心。整个团队也非常愿意顺着这条思路去做决定。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I don't know if you can talk about this in depth, but do you feel like the OpenClaw decision is a part of this, just like, okay, this is not furthering the mission of Anthropic, we need to stop this because it's not working in the way we want it to work?
turns.zh: 不知道你能不能深入聊这个，你觉得 OpenClaw 那个决定是不是也属于这一类？比如，这并不推进 Anthropic 的使命，我们需要叫停，因为它没有按我们希望的方式运作？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think one of the most important things for Anthropic is to grow the number of users that we're able to reach. One of the ways that we're able to do this is with the Claude subscriptions with our first-party products. And so we just very much want to double down on that, but that does come at the expense of third-party products sometimes.
turns.zh: 我认为对 Anthropic 来说最重要的事情之一，是扩大我们能触达的用户数量。实现这一点的方式之一，是通过 Claude 订阅和我们的第一方产品。所以我们非常希望在这上面加倍投入，但这有时确实会以第三方产品为代价。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So we've been talking about Claude Cowork, all these things. Something that I want to make sure people get, and I'm curious just how you use these tools. So there's Claude Code, there's Claude desktop/web, there's Cowork. What's the best way to understand when to use which? When do you use each of these three?
turns.zh: 我们一直在聊 Claude Cowork 之类的东西。有件事我想让大家弄明白，也很好奇你自己是怎么用这些工具的。现在有 Claude Code、Claude 桌面端和网页版、还有 Cowork。怎么理解什么时候该用哪个最好？这三个你分别在什么时候用？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So I tend to use Claude Code in the terminal when I'm just kicking off a one-off coding task, and I want all of the latest features. The CLI is our initial product surface, and it's also the one where our features often land first, and so it's the most powerful of all the tools. So that's what I tend to use when I'm just trying to kick off one or maybe a handful of tasks at a time. I think desktop really shines when you're doing something that requires front end work, and so one thing that I love to do is to use our preview feature.
turns.zh: 我一般在终端里用 Claude Code，当我要启动一个一次性的编码任务，并且想要所有最新功能的时候。CLI 是我们最初的产品形态，也是功能常常最先落地的地方，所以它是所有工具里最强大的。因此当我只想启动一个或者少数几个任务时，我通常会用它。我觉得桌面端在做前端工作的时候特别出色，我很喜欢用我们的预览功能。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So if I'm building a web app, I'll often use Claude Code and desktop. I'll have the preview pane open on the right-hand side so that I can actually see the web app that I'm making in real-time as I'm chatting with Claude. It's also really great for people who want something a bit more graphical. A terminal can feel very unfamiliar to someone who's non-technical. You get a bunch of these scary popups on your machine and you can't click around the way that you're used to in pretty much every other product that you use. So there's a lot of people who just don't feel comfortable in the terminal, and if that's you, I would highly recommend checking out Claude Code on desktop. Desktop is also great for getting an at-a-glance view of everything that's happening. So you can see your CLI terminal sessions in desktop, you can see your other desktop sessions, you can see your sessions that you kicked off on web and mobile. So it's a one-stop control point where you can see all of your tasks.
turns.zh: 比如我在做一个网页应用，我常常会用桌面端的 Claude Code，在右侧开着预览面板，这样我一边跟 Claude 对话，一边就能实时看到我正在做的网页应用。对那些想要更图形化界面的人来说，它也非常好。对非技术人员来说，终端可能很陌生，会弹出一堆吓人的窗口，也没法像用其他产品那样到处点点点。所以很多人在终端里就是不自在，如果你是这样，我强烈建议你试试桌面端的 Claude Code。桌面端还很适合一眼纵览所有正在发生的事情：你能在桌面端看到 CLI 终端里的会话，看到其他桌面端的会话，也能看到你在网页和手机上发起的会话。所以它是一个一站式的控制中心，你可以在这里看到你所有的任务。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think the benefit of web and mobile is that it's really great for kicking things off on the go. So CLI and desktop both require you to be on your local laptop, and this is constraining because sometimes you're out and about, you're touching grass, you're going on a walk and you don't have your laptop open, and I can't count the number of people who I've seen holding their laptop open, like tethered to their phone while they're outside. And this just means that we're missing a product that solves that need. And so for me, what mobile lets you do is kick off these tasks on the go so that you don't need to bring your laptop everywhere and make sure that your laptop's open wherever you are.
turns.zh: 我觉得网页端和手机端的好处，是特别适合在外面随时发起任务。CLI 和桌面端都需要你在本地的笔记本电脑前，这很受限，因为有时候你在外面，在户外走走、散步，没有打开笔记本。我数不清见过多少人把笔记本打开着，连着手机热点，在户外拿着。这说明我们缺少一个满足这种需求的产品。所以对我来说，手机让你能在路上发起这些任务，不必随身带着笔记本，也不用确保无论你在哪里笔记本都开着。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I love that. I've seen people on plane. It's just like such a meme now. Just I need to let this agent finish. I can't shut this down. I need WiFi.
turns.zh: 我太喜欢了。我见过有人在飞机上这样，现在都成梗了：我得让这个智能体跑完，不能关，我需要 WiFi。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Exactly. And then I think for Cowork, the role that this fills is there's a lot of work that everyone does where the output isn't code. So whether that's like getting to Slack zero or inbox zero, or whether that's creating a slide deck for some customer meeting that's coming up, or whether that's writing a quick doc on what the goals of a feature are or what the launch plan for a feature is. All of these tasks produce outputs that are non-code and Cowork is best positioned for that. So the way that I split the products in my mind is if I'm building something where the output is code, I'll use Claude Code or desktop or Claude Code on mobile, and if the output is anything that's not code, I'll use Cowork for it.
turns.zh: 没错。然后说到 Cowork，它扮演的角色是这样的：大家做的很多工作，产出并不是代码。比如把 Slack 清零或者收件箱清零，或者为即将到来的客户会议做一份幻灯片，或者快速写一份文档，说明一个功能的目标是什么，或者一个功能的发布计划是什么。所有这些任务的产出都不是代码，而 Cowork 最适合做这些。所以我在脑子里区分这些产品的方式是：如果我做的东西产出是代码，我就用 Claude Code、桌面端或者手机上的 Claude Code；如果产出不是代码，我就用 Cowork。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: People are just sleeping on the success that Cowork is having. It's just growing incredibly fast, and I think people still don't understand maybe what it's for. And so what if you give us a couple use cases just in your work as a PM? What are some really interesting, maybe unexpected ways you use Cowork to save you time, get more work done?
turns.zh: 大家低估了 Cowork 的成功。它增长得极快，但我觉得大家可能仍然不明白它是干什么的。那你能不能举几个用例，就你作为 PM 的工作而言，有哪些特别有意思、也许出人意料的方式，用 Cowork 帮你省时间、多做事？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: If you are getting started on Cowork, the first thing that you really need to do is connect all the data sources that are relevant to your role because Cowork can only do a great job if it has access to all the context that it needs to be able to curate the output for you. So what that means for me is I connected to my Google Calendar, I connected to my Slack, to my Gmail, to my Google Drive so that it just knows... It has the flexibility to find relevant context, to ask questions, to pull in threads, and this substantially improves the quality of the result. The kinds of things I use it for are like last night we have this Code with Claude conference coming up and there's a few talks that I'm giving there.
turns.zh: 如果你刚开始用 Cowork，首先要做的就是把和你角色相关的所有数据源都连上，因为只有它能访问到所需的全部上下文，Cowork 才能为你做出好的成果。对我来说，就是连上我的 Google Calendar、Slack、Gmail 和 Google Drive，这样它就能灵活地去找相关上下文、提问、拉取讨论串，这会大幅提升结果的质量。我用它做的事情，比如昨晚，我们马上要办 Code with Claude 大会，我在那里有几场演讲。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And one of the talks that we're doing talks about the transition of Claude Code from an assistant to a full-on agent, and one of the things that I wanted to do in this talk was to showcase all of the products that we've been shipping that enable this transition, and also to figure out, okay, what are the success stories that people have had internally that we can use as demos? And so I have my Google Drive connected, I have Slack connected. Alex, who's our product marketer, put together a draft of what the points that he thinks we should cover are.
turns.zh: 其中一场演讲讲的是 Claude Code 从助手转变为完整智能体的过程，我想在这场演讲里展示我们为促成这一转变所上线的全部产品，同时还要弄清楚，内部有哪些成功案例可以拿来做演示。所以我连上了 Google Drive，也连上了 Slack。产品营销同事 Alex 写了一份草稿，列出他认为我们应该涵盖的要点。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so I just fed this all into Cowork. I told Cowork the narrative that I wanted to tell, and it actually just worked for an hour. It looked through Twitter to see what we launched, it looked through our evergreen launch room, it looked in our Claude Code announced channel, which is where our team posts demos of how they've been getting the most value out of Claude Code, and it synthesized all this together to this 20-page deck that I woke up to this morning and I read through it and it was like pretty good. There were a few tweaks, so I did have to give it a round of feedback. I like my slides to have extremely minimal words and it was a little too wordy, but it was far faster than what I would be able to produce. And because Cowork has access to our whole design system, it actually looks like an Anthropic designer put it together. When you visually see it, you're like, "Oh, this is incredibly polished."
turns.zh: 然后我把这些全部丢给了 Cowork。我告诉 Cowork 我想讲的叙事，它就这样干了一个小时。它翻了 Twitter 看我们发布过什么，翻了我们的常青发布群，还看了我们 Claude Code announced 频道，团队会在那里发布他们如何从 Claude Code 获得最大价值的演示。它把这些综合起来，做出了一份 20 页的幻灯片，我今天早上醒来就看到了，读下来觉得相当不错。有几处需要微调，所以我确实给了一轮反馈。我喜欢幻灯片上的字极少，而它写得有点太啰嗦了，但它的速度远比我自己做要快。而且因为 Cowork 能访问我们整个设计系统，成品看起来就像是 Anthropic 的设计师做的，你一眼看过去会觉得：「哇，这太精致了。」

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So these are the kinds of things that are so much faster. Making this slide deck would've taken me hours, but instead it turns out a draft that is actually quite good so that I could focus on making sure that the demos are amazing that we plug into it.
turns.zh: 所以这类事情快太多了。做这份幻灯片本来要花我好几个小时，而现在它直接给出了一份相当不错的草稿，让我能把精力放在确保接入其中的演示足够精彩上。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: This sounds like a dream come true to PMs that... Putting decks together, so annoying.
turns.zh: 这对 PM 们来说简直是梦想成真。做幻灯片太烦人了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It's so slow.
turns.zh: 太慢了。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And I love people will see this deck whenever you present this. This will be out in the world. Obviously it's not the one-shotted version, but you've iterated on it. So just to help people try this for themselves, so step one is connect their... What did you say? Slack. What else do you suggest they connect?
turns.zh: 我也喜欢这一点：你演讲的时候，大家都会看到这份幻灯片，它会公之于众。显然这不是一次生成的版本，而是你迭代过的。那为了帮大家自己试一试，第一步是连上他们的……你刚才说的是什么？Slack。你还建议他们连上什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Slack, Google Calendar, Gmail, GDrive. You should connect your communications tools and where you store your source of truth data for what your team cares about, what you care about and what you're working on.
turns.zh: Slack、Google Calendar、Gmail、GDrive。你应该把沟通工具，以及存放「事实来源」数据的地方都连上，也就是你的团队关心什么、你自己关心什么、你手上在做什么。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Okay. And then what was the prompt roughly that you put in there to generate this deck?
turns.zh: 好的。那你当时输入的提示词大概是什么样的，用来生成这份幻灯片？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So I just wrote make me a slide deck for the code with Claude Conference. This is what our PMM suggested it should cover. This is the current draft that I made that I don't like. This is one that I made manually that I don't like, but I linked it. Can you start by creating a proposed outline with details? Also, make sure it doesn't overlap too much with a keynote talk, which is more important. And then Claude read a bunch of the links that I sent to it and created a proposed outline. So then I read through its proposal and all the different ideas that I had generated for what we could cover, and I just made a decision on what I wanted to actually be in the final deck, and I think this is an example of what the role of the PM still is today.
turns.zh: 我就写了：帮我做一份 Code with Claude 大会的幻灯片。这是我们的 PMM 建议要覆盖的内容，这是我现在写的草稿，但我不满意；这是我手动做的另一版，我也不喜欢，不过我把链接给你了。你能先做一份带细节的大纲提案吗？另外要注意，别和主题演讲重叠太多，主题演讲更重要。然后 Claude 读了我发给它的一堆链接，做出了一份大纲提案。接着我通读了它的提案，还有我之前想到的所有可以讲的点，自己决定最终的幻灯片里到底放什么。我觉得这正是今天产品经理这个角色依然在做的事。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It's like Claude is a great brainstorming partner. It's able to synthesize a massive amount of information really quickly and present all of the possibilities to you, but the role of the PM is still to make the end decision of, okay, what should belong in the final product? So for this, what I ended up deciding was that I wanted the talk to cover the progression from making local tasks successful to making every PR green, to helping engineers land more PRs, and for each of these, which demo would be the most compelling. And then after this decision about the outline, Cowork just went off for a few hours and built the whole slide deck.
turns.zh: Claude 是一个很棒的头脑风暴搭档。它能很快消化海量信息，把所有可能性摆到你面前，但产品经理的角色仍然是做最终决定：好，最终成品里应该放什么？这次我最后决定的是，这场演讲要讲清一条递进的线：先让本地任务成功，再让每个 PR 都变绿，再帮工程师合并更多 PR，而每一步都要选出最有说服力的演示。大纲定下来之后，Cowork 就自己跑了几个小时，把整份幻灯片做完了。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: This is so awesome. What an awesome part of the job to not have to do anymore, and it feels like you're talking to essentially a deck designer that also has actual knowledge about what you've worked on and can make it actually the content what you want it to be, not just make it look really nice. How did you do the design system piece? How does that work? How does it know the design system of Anthropic?
turns.zh: 太棒了。这部分工作居然可以不用再做了，真是太好了。感觉就像你在跟一位幻灯片设计师对话，而且它真的了解你做过的事情，能把内容做成你想要的样子，而不只是把版面做得好看。设计系统那部分你是怎么做的？它怎么知道 Anthropic 的设计系统？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So what I did for this is we actually already have a standardized deck that we use across all of our external engagements. And so I just gave Claude access to that, and so it's able to see what colors we use, what fonts we use, the different kinds of, what's it called, like slide formats that are possible, and so it has 20 of these example slides.
turns.zh: 我们对外所有的活动本来就有一套标准化的幻灯片模板，我只是把它开放给了 Claude。这样它就能看到我们用哪些颜色、哪些字体，还有有哪些版式可用。里面有 20 页这样的示例页。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So give an example, got it. So you upload, here's our template, work from this. Yeah.
turns.zh: 明白，就是说你上传「这是我们的模板，照这个来」。对。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: You can also connect to your Figma MCP if you have your slide format save there and it can pull that in.
turns.zh: 如果你的幻灯片格式存在 Figma 里，你也可以连上 Figma MCP，它能直接把格式拉进来。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Along those lines, something I'm always curious about is what's kind of in your stack of tools as a PM at Anthropic? Obviously Claude Code and Cowork and all the Anthropic tools. What else are you using? What other... Slack you mentioned. Is there anything else?
turns.zh: 顺着这个话题，我一直很好奇，你作为 Anthropic 的产品经理，工具栈里都有什么？显然有 Claude Code、Cowork 和 Anthropic 所有的工具。还有别的吗？你提到了 Slack，还有其他的吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So my stack is pretty heavily Claude Code, Cowork and Slack. Anthropic largely runs on Slack. I feel like it's the core OS of our company. And day-to-day, I would say maybe 30% of my time is pushing the boundaries of what Cowork and Claude Code can do so that I have a very strong sense of what we're not good at, and I spend a lot of time talking with the model to understand why it makes mistakes that it does. We actually have a lot of internal tools that we make. I think one of the things that Claude Code has really unlocked for our entire company is it really lowers the barrier to making any custom app that you want, and so we've seen this surge in personalized work software that people are building for custom use cases instead of using tools that don't perfectly fit the use case.
turns.zh: 我的工具栈主要就是 Claude Code、Cowork 和 Slack。Anthropic 基本上是跑在 Slack 上的，我觉得它是我们公司的核心操作系统。日常来说，我大概有 30% 的时间在不断推动 Cowork 和 Claude Code 的能力边界，这样我就能对我们哪里不行有很清楚的感觉，我也花很多时间和模型对话，去弄清楚它为什么会犯那些错。我们内部还做了很多工具。我觉得 Claude Code 给整个公司带来的一大变化，就是它大大降低了做任何定制应用的门槛，所以我们看到个性化的工作软件大量涌现，大家为自己的具体场景去做，而不是去用那些不太贴合场景的现成工具。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I got to hear more. What are some examples? What are things you've built, other people built that are really popular and useful?
turns.zh: 我想多听听。有哪些例子？你自己做的、或者别人做的，特别受欢迎又好用的有哪些？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: One of the sales folks on Claude Code, he realized he was making these repetitive decks over and over and over again, and so he actually has this web app that he built with the examples of the core Claude Code decks that we know work well, so like a 101, 201 and mastering Claude Code, and then he has a way to input specific customer context that pulls from Salesforce, that pulls from Gong, that pulls from other notes so that we can customize the decks for specific customers. And so we'll pull out things like, okay, this customer is using Bedrock or Claude for enterprise or console, which affects what features are available to them. It'll pull out things like, okay, this customer is concerned about the code review stage of the SLC, and so we'll add a slide about our code review features there. It'll pull out things like, okay, this customer needs to be HIPAA-compliant or needs X, Y, Z security controls, and so we'll make sure to add a slide or two in their deck about that.
turns.zh: Claude Code 的一位销售同事，发现自己总在一遍又一遍地做重复的幻灯片，于是他做了一个网页应用，里面放着我们已知效果不错的几套核心 Claude Code 幻灯片，比如 101、201 和精通 Claude Code。然后他有一个办法输入具体的客户背景，这些信息来自 Salesforce、Gong 和其他笔记，这样我们就能针对具体客户定制幻灯片。比如它会提取出：这个客户用的是 Bedrock、Claude for enterprise 还是 console，这会影响他们能用哪些功能；比如这个客户关心 SDLC 里的代码评审环节，那我们就加一页讲代码评审功能；再比如这个客户需要符合 HIPAA，或者需要 X、Y、Z 这些安全控制，我们就会确保在他们的幻灯片里加上一两页讲这些。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And then for example, if this is a customer that's on Vertex or Bedrock and doesn't want to use Claude for enterprise, then we'll just take out some of the slides that are Claude for enterprise-only features. And so normally this is manual work that could take 20, 30 minutes, and so people will either spend that time doing it or they'll just decide not to do it and use the general deck. With this, it takes a few seconds and you get a tailored deck.
turns.zh: 再比如，如果客户用的是 Vertex 或 Bedrock，不想用 Claude for enterprise，我们就把幻灯片里那些只有 Claude for enterprise 才有的功能删掉。这些事情平时是手工活，可能要花 20、30 分钟，所以大家要么花时间去做，要么干脆不做，直接用通用版幻灯片。有了这个工具，几秒钟就能拿到一份量身定制的幻灯片。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: What's interesting about this Slack is the tool that nobody's... It's just like nobody's trying to create their own. Slack just continues to win, and this is just like the way you describe it as the OS of so many companies. It's so interesting. People talk about Salesforce as just SaaS. We don't need SaaS software anymore. We're going to build our own. It's like Slack is a durable tool that nobody wants to try to compete with and build a better version.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，Slack 是那个没人想去自己做一个的工具。就是没有人想自己造一个。Slack 一直在赢，就像你说的，它是很多公司的操作系统，真的很有意思。大家都在讲 Salesforce 这种就是 SaaS，我们不再需要 SaaS 软件了，我们要自己造。但 Slack 是一个很持久的工具，没人想去和它竞争、做出一个更好的版本。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think it's pretty important communications infrastructure, and I think they do the core task of helping everyone get real-time updates incredibly well.
turns.zh: 我觉得它是非常重要的沟通基础设施，而且在帮每个人实时获取最新动态这件核心任务上，它做得特别好。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Yeah, people hate on Slack, but it's really great at what it's trying to do, and the most cutting-edge teams are hooked on it. It's so interesting.
turns.zh: 对，大家爱吐槽 Slack，但它在自己想做的事情上真的很出色，而且最前沿的团队都离不开它。真的很有意思。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, and I also love how easy they've made to customize it. And so we love making Slack bots and this kind of hackability means that we're able to integrate with Slack the way that we want to. So really appreciate Slack's work on that.
turns.zh: 对，我还很喜欢它定制起来非常方便。我们很爱做 Slack 机器人，这种可玩性让我们可以按自己想要的方式和 Slack 集成。所以真的很感谢 Slack 在这方面的付出。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Time to buy some CRM stock.
turns.zh: 该去买点 CRM 的股票了。

Vanta helps over 15,000 companies like Cursor, Ramp, Duolingo, Snowflake, and Atlassian earn and prove trust with their customers.
