turns.zh: 我非常高兴地向你介绍本季的赞助商 Vanta。Vanta 帮助超过 15,000 家公司，包括 Cursor、Ramp、Duolingo、Snowflake 和 Atlassian，赢得并证明客户对他们的信任。得益于 AI，团队构建和发布产品的速度前所未有，但随之而来的是，你的产品和业务所面临的风险也比以往任何时候都高。我接触的每一位安全负责人，都感到保护组织、保护业务、更不用说保护客户数据的压力越来越重。因为一切变化太快，他们总是在被动应对，只能靠猜来排优先级，只能凑合用过时的方案。Vanta 通过 35 种以上的安全与隐私框架，包括 SOC 2、ISO 27001 和 HIPAA，把合规和风险管理自动化。这能帮公司快速合规，并持续保持合规。比以往任何时候都更是如此，信任有能力成就一家企业，也有能力毁掉一家企业。欢迎到 vanta.com/lenny 了解更多。作为本播客的听众，你还能在 Vanta 立减 1,000 美元。网址是 vanta.com/lenny。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Okay. So you talked about all these different teams and how they use Claude Code and Cowork to operate. Which teams do you find other than engineering... Imagine engineering is the biggest token spender, but if not, that'd be really interesting. What's the second place function right now for tokens?
turns.zh: 好。你刚才讲了这么多团队是怎么用 Claude Code 和 Cowork 来工作的。除了工程之外，你觉得哪些团队用得最多？我想工程应该是 token 花得最多的，但如果不是，那就更有意思了。目前 token 消耗排第二的职能是哪个？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Oh, Applied AI is amazing at pushing the boundaries of what Claude Code and Cowork can do. A lot of our Applied AI team spends time with our customers helping them adopt our API, and so sometimes our Applied AI team will, for example, make prototypes on behalf of these customers, which Claude Code makes so much faster than it used to do. They also have the dual goal of needing to manage a lot of customer comms, a lot of customer inbound and historical context, call notes, and so they're both extremely heavy on Cowork and on Claude Code.
turns.zh: 哦，Applied AI 特别厉害，一直在突破 Claude Code 和 Cowork 的能力边界。Applied AI 团队里很多人把时间花在陪客户采用我们的 API 上，所以有时候他们会替客户做原型，Claude Code 让这件事比以前快太多了。他们还有另一个目标，就是要处理大量的客户沟通、大量的客户来信，还有历史背景、通话记录，所以他们对 Cowork 和 Claude Code 都是重度使用。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And just to understand Applied AI, is that forward to play engineering sort of role? How would most people describe what the Applied AI team is doing?
turns.zh: 我确认一下，Applied AI 是不是类似前置部署工程师（forward deployed engineer）那样的角色？大多数人会怎么描述 Applied AI 团队在做的事？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, it's helping our customers adopt the latest API and model features across their company, both for powering their company's products and also for internal acceleration.
turns.zh: 是的，就是帮我们的客户在整个公司范围内采用最新的 API 和模型功能，既用于驱动他们公司的产品，也用于内部提效。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Got it. So it's like customer success, go to marketing, kind of for deploy engineering sort of thing.
turns.zh: 明白了。所以有点像客户成功、市场推广，再加上部署工程这类角色。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Exactly. It's like a very technical go to-market person.
turns.zh: 没错。就是一个技术性非常强的市场推广人员。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Got it. Okay, awesome. So you're saying that might be the second org that uses the most tokens?
turns.zh: 明白。好的，太棒了。所以你是说，他们可能是第二大 token 用户组织？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah. And then we also see them pushing the boundaries of what Cowork can do. So for example, if... So a lot of these folks cover multiple customers and in any given day can have five to 10 customer engagements on a high day, and so what they often use Cowork to do is the night before, they'll ask it to summarize, okay, what are all my customer meetings that are coming up the next day? What are all the things that this customer has asked me for? What's top of mind for them? What are the action items from the past meetings? And Cowork will just put together this dossier, this brief of what they should be aware of going into the next meeting. And Cowork can also research answers. So if a customer asks, "Okay, when is feature X going to launch?" Cowork can help the Applied AI person research through Slack to get the latest ETA, add that to the notes so that during the customer call, the Applied AI person has the absolute latest. And these are just workflows that people are building for themselves and sharing with other people on their team.
turns.zh: 对。而且我们还看到他们在不断突破 Cowork 的能力边界。比如，这些人很多都要对接多个客户，忙的时候一天可以有五到十场客户会议，所以他们经常用 Cowork 来做的事是，前一天晚上让它总结：我明天有哪些客户会议？这个客户都向我要过什么？他们现在最关心什么？之前几次会议留下了哪些待办事项？然后 Cowork 就会整理出一份档案，一份简报，写明进入下一场会议前应该知道什么。Cowork 还能帮忙查答案。比如客户问「功能 X 什么时候上线？」，Cowork 可以帮 Applied AI 的同事去 Slack 里查最新的预计时间，加进笔记里，这样客户通话时，Applied AI 的同事手上就有最新的信息。这些都是大家为自己搭建的工作流，并且在团队里互相分享。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: So cool. Something that kind of this question, this trend, I don't know, question topic comes up a lot recently, which is tokens spend exceeding people's salary where people just use AI and it costs more than how much they're making. Are there any numbers floating around Anthropic of just how much tokens spend, say, engineers spend, I don't know, a month, a day or PMs, anything like that?
turns.zh: 太酷了。最近这个话题经常被提到：token 花费超过人的薪水，也就是有人用 AI 花的钱比他挣的还多。Anthropic 内部有没有一些大概的数字，比如工程师一个月或一天花多少 token，或者产品经理花多少，诸如此类？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It is clear to us that as the models get better, people delegate far more tasks to it and they spend a lot more hours in tools like Claude Code and Cowork, and so we do see the token cost per engineer or per any knowledge worker increase every time that there's a model jump or a substantial product improvement. I think it's still much lower than what the average engineer salary is, but we see the percentage increasing over time.
turns.zh: 我们很清楚的一点是，模型越强，人们就会把多得多的任务委托给它，在 Claude Code 和 Cowork 这类工具里待的时间也长得多。所以每次模型有大的飞跃，或者产品有明显改进，我们都会看到每位工程师、或者每位知识工作者的 token 成本上升。我觉得它仍然远低于工程师的平均薪资，但我们看到这个比例在逐渐上升。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: It's such an interesting... We talked about how you have access to the most cutting-edge models and other advantage of working Anthropic, I believe you guys have basically unlimited tokens. You can use as much as you want. Is that right?
turns.zh: 这很有意思……我们刚才聊到你们能用到最前沿的模型，我想在 Anthropic 工作的另一个优势是，你们基本上有无限的 token，想用多少用多少。是这样吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: We can use a lot of tokens. Some people do run into limits, so-
turns.zh: 我们可以用很多 token。有些人确实会碰到上限，所以——

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Okay, there's a limit. Okay. Boris, shut it down. Okay. It's so interesting how many advantages come from having the most advanced model. It's such an interesting flywheel that starts to kick in.
turns.zh: 好吧，还是有上限的。好。Boris，关掉它。好。有最先进的模型会带来这么多优势，真的很有意思，这是一个开始转起来的飞轮。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think we also believe a lot in empowering our internal teams to build as fast as possible, and we also trust that everyone understands how much capacity that serving these models truly costs, and we trust our team to use the tokens responsibly. So it's very frowned upon to waste tokens, but we do trust individuals to make that judgment call.
turns.zh: 我们也非常相信要让内部团队尽可能快地去构建，同时我们相信每个人都明白，服务这些模型的算力到底要花多少钱，所以我们信任团队会负责任地使用 token。浪费 token 是很不被提倡的，但我们确实信任每个人自己做判断。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Awesome. Coming back to the PM role, we talked a little bit about this, but I think this will be really interesting for people to hear. Just what I want to understand is what do you think are the emerging skills that PMs need to develop/you most look for, AI companies most look for when they're hiring PMs these days?
turns.zh: 太好了。回到产品经理这个角色，我们聊过一点，但我觉得这对大家会很有意思。我想了解的是，你认为产品经理需要培养哪些新兴技能？还有，现在 AI 公司招产品经理时最看重什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think the hardest skill is being able to define what the product should look like a month from now. I think there's a lot of ambiguity in what models are capable of in that timeline and how user behavior will change, but I think there are patterns that the best PMs can see based on how users are abusing the limits of the existing product and the best PMs can sense that, can set a direction and can steadily execute towards it and change the path if the model capabilities are much better than or worse than what they'd originally expected. I think it is very hard to be the right amount of AGI-pilled because I think everyone can see this future where the models are extremely smart and can do almost everything, in which case you actually don't need that complicated a product, you can actually just have a text box again where you tell the model what you want and it's so smart that it can add any tool or add any integration that it needs to get the job done. It knows when it's uncertain, it can ask clarifying questions.
turns.zh: 我觉得最难的技能，是能够定义一个月之后产品应该是什么样子。在这个时间跨度里，模型能做什么、用户行为会怎么变，都有很多不确定性。但我认为有一些规律，最优秀的产品经理能从用户如何「滥用」现有产品的极限中看出来，他们能感知到这些，能定下方向，稳步朝它推进，并且在模型能力比原先预期好很多或差很多的时候调整路径。我觉得要做到恰到好处的「AGI 信仰」非常难，因为每个人都能想象这样一个未来：模型极其聪明，几乎什么都能做，那样你其实不需要那么复杂的产品，你可以又回到一个文本框，告诉模型你想要什么，它聪明到可以自己加上完成任务所需的任何工具、任何集成。它知道自己什么时候不确定，会提出澄清问题。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: It's kind of very easy to build the product for the super AGI strong model. I think the hard thing is figuring out for the current model, how do you elicit the maximum capability? How do you help users go get onto the golden path? How do you guide users to interact with the model's strengths and patch its weaknesses? This skill is pretty rare.
turns.zh: 为那个超级 AGI 的强大模型去做产品，其实很容易。难的是，针对当前的模型，怎么把它的最大能力激发出来？怎么帮用户走上那条「黄金路径」？怎么引导用户去发挥模型的长处、弥补它的短板？这种技能相当稀缺。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And how do you build that skill? Is it just using each... Basically understanding the limits of each model? You talked about taste, understanding, having taste into what the model maybe is capable of, what it's great and not great to at, where it's changed?
turns.zh: 那这个技能怎么培养？是不是就是每个模型都去用，基本上去了解每个模型的极限？你提到过品味，也就是对模型可能有什么能力、哪方面强哪方面弱、哪里变了，要有品味？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Think it's spending a ton of time talking and using the model. One of the things I really like to do is to ask the model to introspect on its own behaviors. So sometimes when I notice that the model does something unexpected, like for example, there's situations where the model will make a front end change and run tests, but not actually use the UI. It's actually pretty useful to ask the model to reflect on why I did this, and sometimes they'll say that, "Hey, there was something confusing in the system prompt," or, "I didn't realize that the front end verification was part of this task," Or, "Hey, I delegated the verification to this subagent and the subagent didn't do the test and I didn't check its work." A lot of times just being very curious about why the model made the decision that it did will show you what misled it so that you can fix the harness in order to close this gap.
turns.zh: 我觉得就是花大量的时间跟模型聊、用模型。我很喜欢做的一件事，是让模型对它自己的行为做反思。有时候我发现模型做了出乎意料的事，比如，有些情况下模型改了前端，跑了测试，却没有真的去用界面。这时候让模型反思一下「你为什么这么做」就很有用，有时它会说：「嘿，系统提示词里有个地方让我困惑」，或者「我没意识到前端验证也是这个任务的一部分」，或者「我把验证委托给了这个子智能体，而子智能体没有做测试，我也没有检查它的工作」。很多时候，只要对模型为什么做出那个决定保持好奇，就能看出是什么误导了它，这样你就可以修复运行框架，把这个缺口补上。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: The other thing that helps is to figure out who are the users who you trust the most to give you accurate feedback about the model. Usually there's a handful of people who are much better than others at articulating what makes a specific model or model harness combination good, and there's a lot of people who will give you feedback, but not everyone's feedback is as qualified. And so finding a group of those five people you trust is really important for getting very fast feedback. I think the third thing that is useful, but not everyone loves doing is building evals. You don't need to build hundreds of evals for them to be useful. Just building 10 great evals is important for helping the team quantify what the goal is and what their progress towards it is and what they're missing, and so I think evals is this underappreciated thing that more PMs, more engineers should be working on.
turns.zh: 另一件有帮助的事，是弄清楚你最信任哪些用户，能给你关于模型的准确反馈。通常总有那么几个人，在说清楚某个模型、或者某个模型加运行框架的组合好在哪里这件事上，比别人强得多；很多人都会给你反馈，但不是每个人的反馈都同样靠谱。所以找到你信任的那五个人，对快速拿到反馈非常重要。第三件有用的事是做评测，不过不是每个人都喜欢做。你不需要做几百个评测才有用，只要做出 10 个好的评测，就能帮团队量化目标是什么、朝它走到了哪一步、还缺什么。所以我觉得评测是一件被低估的事，更多的产品经理、更多的工程师都应该去做。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: We've covered evals a bunch. There's this trend of just like, that is the future of product management's writing evals because essentially it's what does success look like. Okay, cool. Let me actually concretely define it and then we'll know. How much of your time are you spending writing evals, would you say?
turns.zh: 评测我们已经聊过不少了。现在有一种趋势，认为产品管理的未来就是写评测，因为本质上就是定义成功是什么样子：好，让我具体地把它定义出来，然后我们就知道了。你自己大概有多少时间花在写评测上？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think the importance of evals varies a bit based on the feature that you're working on or what the problem you're trying to solve is. So there are a lot of folks on our team who do spend a lot of time working on evals. We have a small pod of folks who collaborate very closely with research to more precisely understand our Claude Code behaviors and what the largest areas of improvement are and trying to measure those pretty concretely. I personally jump into evals when there's a feature that I think needs a bit more product definition, and often the output of this is, "Okay, here are five evals that I made. This is how you run them. These are the ones that succeed and these are the ones that don't, and this is the prompt that I've used to increase the success rate." It varies a lot though based on the exact feature. Not every feature needs it, but I think features such as memory benefit a lot from it.
turns.zh: 我觉得评测的重要性会因你做的功能、或者你要解决的问题而有所不同。我们团队里有不少人确实在评测上花很多时间。我们有一个小组，和研究团队紧密合作，更精确地理解 Claude Code 的各种行为，以及最大的改进空间在哪里，并尽量具体地去衡量。我自己会在某个功能需要更多产品定义的时候跳进去做评测，通常产出是这样的：「这是我做的五个评测，这是运行方法，这些通过了，这些没通过，这是我用来提高成功率的提示词。」不过这非常取决于具体功能。不是每个功能都需要，但我觉得像记忆这样的功能就很受益。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: This point you made about people being very good at evaluating models so interesting. It's almost like a human eval of just like, okay, they understand where it's spiking, where it's maybe lacking. Is there anyone specific that you want to shout out that's very good at this?
turns.zh: 你说有些人特别擅长评估模型，这点很有意思。这几乎就像是一种人工评测：他们能理解模型哪里表现突出、哪里可能不足。你有没有想特别点名的、在这方面很强的人？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Two people who I think are incredible at this are, one, Amanda, who molds Claude's character. It's just such a hard role because the task is so ambiguous. Even coding is easier because you can verify the success, whereas crafting the character requires a very strong sense of conviction in who Claude should be, and I think she has an incredible ability to not only mold the character, but also to articulate what the goals are, what the character, what's successful and what's not. The other group of people who I really trust is just the Claude Code team.
turns.zh: 我觉得有两位在这方面非常了不起。第一位是 Amanda，她负责塑造 Claude 的性格。这个角色太难了，因为任务本身非常模糊。就连写代码都更容易，因为成功与否可以验证；而塑造性格，需要对 Claude 应该成为什么样的人有非常坚定的信念。我觉得她不仅有塑造性格的卓越能力，还能清楚地表达目标是什么，什么样的性格算成功、什么不算。另一群我非常信任的人，就是 Claude Code 团队。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So we often have team lunches and whenever there's a new model we're testing, one of the fastest ways for us to get feedback is to just at these team lunches, just go to every single person and just be like, "Hey, what is your vibe on the model?" And oftentimes we'll get feedback like, "Okay, this model is not fully explaining its thinking. It's too abrupt," or like, "Hey, this model just loves writing a ton of memories, but we're not sure if the memories are high quality or not," or some people will notice that, "Okay, this model loves to test itself, which is great, or this model isn't testing itself enough." So that informs what data we look at to verify, okay, is this a larger pattern? So we have a ton of data, but it is very hard to extract insights, and so the feedback from this group helps us inform, okay, what are the hypotheses we want to test, and then we're able to extract data to test that.
turns.zh: 我们团队经常一起吃午饭，每次有新模型要测试，最快拿到反馈的办法之一，就是趁着午饭挨个儿问每个人：「嘿，你觉得这个模型的感觉怎么样？」常常会听到这样的反馈：「这个模型没把思考过程讲清楚，太突兀了」，或者「这个模型特别爱写一大堆记忆，但我们不确定这些记忆质量高不高」，也有人会发现「这个模型喜欢自己测试自己，这很好」，或者「这个模型测试自己测得不够」。这些反馈会告诉我们该去看哪些数据，来验证这是不是一个更普遍的规律。我们手上有海量数据，但很难从中提炼出洞察，所以这个小圈子的反馈能帮我们确定：到底想验证哪些假设？然后我们再去提取数据来检验。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: This point you made about the character of Claude, I had Ben Mann on the podcast, co-founder, and he talked about this, just the character, the constitution of Claude is such an important part of Claude. And I didn't realize until afterwards just with OpenClaw actually, one of the reasons people are sad is the personality of your Claude is... Because Claude's personality is so good and fun and interesting unlike other models. And the way he put it is the personality is what makes Claude so good at so many things. It feels like this trivial side thing. Okay, it's going to be funny and interesting and talk in a fun way, but it's so core to the success of Claude. Is there anything get shared there about just what people may not understand about why the character, as you described, and the personality is so key?
turns.zh: 你说的 Claude 的性格这一点，我之前请过 Ben Mann 上节目，他是联合创始人，他也讲到了这个：Claude 的性格、它的宪法，是 Claude 非常重要的一部分。其实直到后来，尤其是 OpenClaw 这件事，我才意识到，人们感到难过的原因之一，就是你们的 Claude 的性格……因为 Claude 的性格那么好、那么有趣，和其他模型不一样。他的说法是，正是这种性格让 Claude 在这么多事情上都那么出色。这看起来像是一件无关紧要的小事，不就是幽默一点、有趣一点、说话好玩一点嘛，但它其实是 Claude 成功的核心。关于为什么你说的这种特质和性格如此关键，是不是有什么人们可能没意识到的地方，你能分享一下吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: When you reflect on everyone you've worked with, there's just some people where you're like, "I really like their energy. I really like their vibe," and when people think about Claude and Claude Code, this is one of the things that people bring up the most where they just really love that Claude, it's lighthearted and fun, but it also is extremely confident at your task. People really like that Claude's low ego, and so if you tell it, "Hey, you did this thing wrong." It's truly sorry. It's like, "Oh, shoot. Thanks for telling me. Let me fix it. Let's work together." It's also very positive. So if you're feeling like, "Oh, this is an insurmountable task. I don't know how to get started," Claude is like, "Okay, it's okay. These are the steps that I think we should take. Do you want me to get started on it for you?"
turns.zh: 回想一下你共事过的所有人，总有一些人让你觉得「我就是喜欢他们的气场，喜欢他们那种感觉」。人们谈起 Claude 和 Claude Code 的时候，这是被提到最多的点之一：大家就是特别喜欢 Claude，它轻松有趣，但在你的任务上又极其自信。人们喜欢 Claude 的低自我：你对它说「嘿，这件事你做错了」，它是真的会抱歉，会说「哎呀，谢谢你告诉我，我来改，我们一起搞定」。它也非常积极。比如你觉得「这任务太难了，我不知道从哪儿下手」，Claude 会说：「没关系，我觉得可以按这几步来。要我先帮你开个头吗？」

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think part of what makes a great Coworker is this positivity, this bias towards action, this ability to give you earnest feedback, not just agreeing with every single thing that you say, and so we try to imbue this into Claude because we think it makes it a lot more enjoyable to work with.
turns.zh: 我觉得一个出色的同事，就该有这种积极的态度、这种偏向行动的倾向，还能给你真诚的反馈，而不是你说什么它都附和。所以我们努力把这些特质注入 Claude，因为我们觉得这会让和它共事愉快得多。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: There's something I want to come back to. You talked about how when new models come out, you often have to revisit things you've built. That's so interesting and so frustrating maybe, just like, "Oh, Goddammit it. Reshipped this thing, now I have to rethink it." Talk about just how often you have to come back with a new model and they're like, "Okay, we have to redo this product that we launched a few months ago."
turns.zh: 有件事我想回过头聊聊。你说到新模型发布的时候，经常要回头重新审视之前做过的东西。这挺有意思的，也可能挺让人崩溃的，就像「天哪，刚发布的东西，现在又得重新想」。聊聊你们多久就得因为新模型来一次，然后说「好，几个月前上线的这个产品得重做了」？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: A lot of the changes that we make with a new model is removing features that are no longer needed. So a lot of times we add features to the product as a crutch for the model because it's not naturally doing itself. So the classic example for this is the to do list. When we first launched Claude Code, people would ask it to do these larger factors and Claude Code would say, "Okay, cool. I need to change these 20 call sites," and it would go and change five of them and then stop. And then we were like, "Okay, how do we force it to remember to get every single one of these 20?" And so Sid on our team was like, "Okay, what if we just think about what a human would do? A human would make a list of everything that they need to change. Similar to how in VS Code, you would look up all the call sites and it would be a list on the left side and you would go through them one by one and replace all. How do we give this kind of a tool to Claude?"
turns.zh: 新模型带来的很多改动，其实是删掉不再需要的功能。很多时候，我们给产品加功能，是给模型当拐杖，因为模型自己没法自然地做到。最典型的例子就是待办清单。刚推出 Claude Code 的时候，人们让它做比较大的重构，Claude Code 会说：「好的，我需要修改这 20 处调用点」，结果它改了五处就停了。于是我们想，怎么才能逼它记得把这 20 处全部改完？团队里的 Sid 就说：「我们想想人会怎么做。人会把需要改的东西列成一张清单，就像在 VS Code 里，你会查出所有调用点，它们在左侧排成一列，你一个个过，再全部替换。我们怎么把这样的工具给 Claude？」

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And so he added the to do list and we found that with that, Claude was actually able to fix all these 20 call sites. But then with Opus 4 and later models, we realized that we didn't need to force it to use this to do list, it would naturally use itself. For the earlier models, we had to keep reminding it, "Hey, did you finish everything on the to do list? You can't finish until you're done with everything on the to do list." And for the later models, without prompting, it's just naturally thinks to do everything on the to do list. These days, the to do list is still nice to have as a user because then you can more clearly see what Claude is working on. But honestly, it's such a de-emphasized part of the product right now that the model may use it, the model may not use it. It's really not necessary for it to make thorough changes anymore.
turns.zh: 于是他加上了待办清单，我们发现有了它，Claude 真的能把这 20 处调用点全改完。但到了 Opus 4 和之后的模型，我们发现不用再强制它用待办清单了，它自己就会自然地用。对更早的模型，我们得不停提醒它：「嘿，清单上的事都做完了吗？清单上的事没做完之前，你不能结束。」而对后来的模型，不用提示，它自然就会想着把清单上的事全做完。现在待办清单对用户来说仍然不错，因为你能更清楚地看到 Claude 在做什么。但说实话，它在产品里已经是个被淡化的部分了，模型可能用，也可能不用，它对于让模型把改动做彻底，已经没那么必要了。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I forget who said this on the podcast, that the model will eat your harness for breakfast, and what I'm hearing here is essentially you remove things over time that you've had to add on top of the model where it was not operating the way you wanted. And essentially, as the models get smarter, it becomes simpler and simpler for it just to do the thing you want it to do.
turns.zh: 我忘了是谁在节目里说过，模型会把你的运行框架当早餐吃掉。我从你这里听到的意思基本上就是：你会随着时间推移，把当初为了纠正模型不按你想要的方式工作而加在它上面的东西逐步拿掉。而随着模型越来越聪明，让它去做你想做的事就变得越来越简单。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah. We can remove a lot of prompting interventions every time the model gets smarter. And we actually do this every time we launch a model, we read through the entire system prompt and we reflect on, okay, for each of these sections, does the model really need this reminder anymore, and if not, we'll remove it. The most exciting thing that new models unlocks though is just entirely new features. So there's a lot of features that we've been testing out with prior models and the accuracy wasn't high enough for us to want to launch them, and so one example of this is code review. We tried to build a code review product a few times and we've launched simpler versions of code review, which is the /codereview command in the past, and it was only with the most recent models that we felt like, okay, this code review is so good that our engineering team relies on this code review to pass before we merge PRs.
turns.zh: 对。每次模型变聪明，我们都能去掉很多提示词层面的干预。而且我们每次发布模型，都会把整个系统提示词通读一遍，逐段反思：这一段，模型还需要这个提醒吗？如果不需要，就删掉。不过新模型带来的最令人兴奋的，还是全新的功能。有很多功能，我们在之前的模型上试过，但准确率不够高，不足以让我们发布。一个例子就是代码审查。我们试着做过几次代码审查产品，之前也发布过比较简单的版本，也就是 /codereview 命令，直到最近的这批模型，我们才觉得：好，这个代码审查现在够好了，好到我们的工程团队在合并 PR 之前，要依赖这个代码审查通过。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And we found that this was... We've always dreamed of Claude being able to be a reliable code reviewer that we can confidently feel catches the majority of bugs, and it was only with Opus 4.5 and 4.6, and Sonnet 4.6 that we felt like, okay, we are now able to run multiple code review agents simultaneously to traverse the entirety of the code base and to synthesize a set of real issues that an engineer needs to address before merge. And so this is a new capability that the newest models have unlocked.
turns.zh: 我们一直梦想着让 Claude 成为一个可靠的代码审查者，能让我们有信心地认为它抓出了大多数 bug。直到 Opus 4.5 和 4.6，还有 Sonnet 4.6，我们才觉得：好，现在可以同时运行多个代码审查智能体，遍历整个代码库，再综合出一份工程师在合并前必须处理的真实问题清单。所以，这是最新的模型解锁的一项新能力。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: This is another trend that is very common on this podcast of build something that will possibly be possible in the next six months, be kind of at the edge of what's working sort of, and then it'll catch up and then it'll be an amazing product and you'll be ahead of everyone.
turns.zh: 这是这档播客上很常见的另一个趋势：去做一个未来六个月内有可能实现的东西，让它处在刚好能用、又不太好用的边缘，等模型追上来，它就会变成一个很棒的产品，你就领先所有人了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, exactly. It's pretty important to build products that don't necessarily work yet so that you know, okay, what is missing for this product to work? And then with the newest model, you can just swap it into the prototype you've already made and see, okay, does this new model close that gap?
turns.zh: 对，没错。做一些暂时还不太能用的产品，其实很重要，这样你就知道这个产品到底缺什么才能跑通。等新模型出来，你直接把它换进你已经做好的原型里，看看这个新模型能不能补上那块缺口。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: How much are you able to speak to just where things are going with Claude and Cowork as the vision of it? I imagine you don't want to give away too much about the goal, but it feels like there's all these awesome features being added on top, dispatch, control from phone and all these mobile app, all these things. What's kind of just a way to understand the vision for all these things long-term?
turns.zh: 关于 Claude 和 Cowork 的愿景，也就是它们接下来的方向，你能说多少？我想你不会透露太多目标，但感觉上面不断有很棒的功能加进来，比如 dispatch、手机远程控制，还有各种移动应用。要怎么理解这些东西长期的愿景呢？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: We think about this in terms of building blocks. So for both Claude Code and Cowork, the core building block is making individual tasks successful. So you wanted to produce some output, you give it a prompt description. Is it able to consistently produce acceptable output that you're able to either merge or share with your colleagues or external audience? So the task is the core building block. As the models get smarter, the task access rate gets a lot higher, and then we see people moving towards doing multiple tasks at the same time. So multi-Claudeing was this big thing towards the end of 2025, and it's only increased since then. And so we see this as, okay, great. One task works, and now you can do six tasks at a time. As the models get even smarter, the way that we are extrapolating this is, okay, next, maybe you're going to run 50 Claudes at a time or hundreds of Claudes at a time, and so what is the infrastructure we need to build to enable that?
turns.zh: 我们是用「积木」的思路来想这件事的。对 Claude Code 和 Cowork 来说，最核心的积木都是让单个任务成功。你想产出某个结果，给它一段提示词描述，它能不能稳定地产出合格的结果，让你可以合并，或者分享给同事或外部受众？所以任务是最核心的积木。随着模型变聪明，任务的成功率大大提高，我们就看到人们开始同时做多个任务。「多开 Claude」在 2025 年底成了一股大潮，此后只增不减。所以我们的看法是：很好，一个任务能跑通了，现在你可以同时做六个。等模型再聪明一些，我们推断下一步，你也许会同时运行 50 个甚至上百个 Claude，那我们需要搭建什么样的基础设施来支撑这件事？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: At that point, you're probably not going to run everything locally on your machine anymore. There's just not enough RAM to do it. And so we're thinking about how do we make it easier for you to manage all these? These will probably run remotely. How do we build the interface so that you as a human know which tasks you need to look into? How do we make sure that the agent is fully verifying its work so that when you look at a task and it says it's done, you can very quickly verify and fully trust that it is done to your spec. And how do we make sure that this process is self-improving so that when you do see a task that isn't done to your liking, you can give it feedback and the model will know for every future run to incorporate that feedback so it never makes that mistake again? So this is the progression that we're bringing our users along for.
turns.zh: 到那个阶段，你大概不会再把所有东西都跑在自己机器上了，内存根本不够。所以我们在想，怎么让你更容易管理这一切？这些任务多半会在远端运行。我们怎么设计界面，让你作为人类知道该去看哪些任务？怎么确保智能体充分验证了自己的工作，这样当你看到一个任务显示已完成时，可以很快验证，并完全相信它确实按你的要求完成了？还有，怎么确保这个过程能自我改进，这样当你看到某个任务没做到你满意时，可以给它反馈，而模型在之后的每一次运行里都会记得吸收这条反馈，永远不再犯同样的错？这就是我们要带着用户一路走过的演进路径。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: There's a lot of people listening, a lot of product managers, a lot of maybe founders, a lot of other cross-functional folks listening. There's a lot of worry about just how their role... Just the future of their careers. What advice would you have for just people to not just survive this transition to this very AI-driven world, but to be really successful to essentially just to thrive in this future? What are just things people need to hear, need to be doing?
turns.zh: 现在听众里有很多产品经理，很多创始人，也有很多其他跨职能的朋友，大家都很担心自己的角色，担心自己职业的未来。你对大家有什么建议，不只是帮他们挺过这场向 AI 驱动世界的转变，而是真正活得出色，在这样的未来里茁壮成长？有哪些话是大家需要听到的，有哪些事是大家需要去做的？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think AI gives everybody a ton more leverage than they used to, and so I would push you towards anytime you realize that you're doing some manual task multiple times, think about how you can use Claude Code, Cowork, or other AI tools to automate that for you. Most people have creative parts of their job that they absolutely love and then tedious parts of their job that they really hate doing. I think the beauty of AI is that it can do those tedious parts for you. It can learn from every time that you've done that manual task and generalize and then run it automatically and so that you can focus on the creative parts and that means you can do a lot more than you used to be able to do.
turns.zh: 我觉得 AI 给了每个人比以前多得多的杠杆。所以我会建议你，每当发现自己在重复做某件手动任务时，就想一想怎么用 Claude Code、Cowork 或其他 AI 工具把它自动化。大多数人的工作里，都有自己特别热爱的创造性部分，也有特别讨厌的繁琐部分。我觉得 AI 的美妙之处就在于，它可以替你做那些繁琐的部分。它能从你每一次手动做这件事的过程中学习，然后加以泛化，自动运行，这样你就可以专注在创造性的部分，也就意味着你能做的事比以前多得多。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: So I think my immediate push for people is figure out the repetitive parts that you can pass to Claude, iterate on those automations until the success rate is very high, and then focus on, okay, what more can you be doing for your team, for your product, for your company that people haven't had the bandwidth to pick up so far, or what is that pet project that you always thought the company should do that you've never had bandwidth to do? If AI can take care of the grunt work, then you have this extra 20% time now that you might not have before. So my push is to lean into these tools, hand off the work that you're not excited to do, figure out how it can accelerate you, and then as a result, you'll be able to do so much more.
turns.zh: 所以我给大家的当务之急建议是：找出那些重复性的工作交给 Claude，不断迭代这些自动化，直到成功率很高，然后去想：我还能为团队、为产品、为公司做些什么，是之前大家没精力去做的？或者，你一直觉得公司应该做、却从来没精力做的那个小项目是什么？如果 AI 能把苦力活包下来，你就多出了 20% 的时间，这是你以前可能没有的。所以我的建议是：拥抱这些工具，把你不想做的工作交出去，想办法让它帮你提速，这样你就能做成多得多的事。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Something core to what you just shared, which I fully agree with is find problems to solve with AI. There's all this potential what all these tools can do. For a lot of people, the hardest part is just like, "What should I actually do?" And what you're saying here is just pay attention to things that you are doing constantly you can automate, pay attention to just ideas that have been floating around that you haven't had time to do. It's basically it's like solve a problem for yourself is kind of the core advice there.
turns.zh: 你刚才说的有个核心，我完全同意，就是要去找可以用 AI 解决的问题。这些工具有这么多潜力，对很多人来说，最难的反而是「我到底该做什么」。你的意思是，留意那些你一直在做、可以自动化的事，留意那些一直在脑子里转、却没时间做的想法。基本上，核心建议就是：先为自己解决一个问题。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Exactly. I would also push listeners towards focusing on bringing your automations from, okay, this is a cool concept to like, hey, this actually works 100% of the time. Sometimes I see users trying to automate something, getting it to 90, 95% accuracy and then giving up on it, and if an automation doesn't work 100% of the time, it's not really an automation, and that last five to 10% does take more time. Also, building the automation is often a lot slower than you doing it yourself. I would encourage listeners to put in that time to scope some automation that you really want to get to 100%, put in the elbow grease to teach Claude your preferences, to give it feedback so that it can improve its skill so that it can get to that 100%, and then really then you'll be able to rely on it. There's just not much value in a 95% there automation.
turns.zh: 没错。我还想建议听众，把你的自动化从「这是个酷炫的概念」推进到「它真的能百分之百奏效」。我有时看到用户尝试自动化某件事，做到 90%、95% 的准确率就放弃了。但一个自动化如果不能百分之百奏效，就算不上真正的自动化，而最后那 5% 到 10% 确实要花更多时间。而且，搭建自动化往往比你自己动手做慢得多。我鼓励听众花这个时间，选一个你真心想做到 100% 的自动化，下功夫去教 Claude 你的偏好，给它反馈，让它改进自己的技能，最终做到 100%，到那时你才真正能依赖它。一个 95% 的自动化，其实没多大价值。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I am super guilty of that. This is really good advice for me.
turns.zh: 这一点我太中招了。这个建议对我真的很有用。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I am guilty of this too. I've been teaching Cowork to try to get me to inbox zero for Gmail, and it has been very time-consuming and it is definitely not there as you probably realize.
turns.zh: 我也是。我一直在教 Cowork 帮我把 Gmail 收件箱清到零，这个过程非常耗时，你大概也猜到了，它到现在还没做到。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Yeah. Funny enough, that's exactly where my mind goes. I have this workflow I set up where every email I get, it looks for things that are spammy, which is just all these like, "Hey, can I come on your podcast?" Or, "What about this?" All these things, I'm just like, "I don't have time for these sorts of things," and I have it categorized it into a folder called Spammy and it's just like, it's 95% great, but then there's like, oh, wow, I missed an email because it went in there. So this is a good push for me to like, I'm going to work on this. I'm going to get it to perfect.
turns.zh: 是啊，说来好笑，我的脑子也是直接想到这个。我设置了一套流程，每封邮件进来，它会找出那些垃圾味的，比如各种「嘿，我能上你的播客吗？」或者「你看这个怎么样？」之类的，我就想「这些事我没时间处理」，于是让它把这些邮件归到一个叫 Spammy 的文件夹里。它做到 95% 都很好，但时不时就会冒出一句「哇，我漏掉了一封邮件，因为它被分到那里面去了」。所以这对我是个很好的推动：我要在这上面下功夫，把它做到完美。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah. We also are working on making the flow for customizing these commands a lot easier because right now I think you have to know too many concepts. You have to know to define a skill, you have to know to use this skill and give it feedback, and then you have to know to tell Cowork to update the skill based on all the feedback that you gave, and then you also have to know where to read the skill to make sure that the feedback was incorporated the way that you want. It's also our job to make this flow really seamless so that it doesn't feel painful to do.
turns.zh: 对。我们也在努力让自定义这些命令的流程变得简单得多，因为现在我觉得你需要懂的概念太多了。你得知道去定义一个技能，得知道怎么用这个技能并给它反馈，然后得知道告诉 Cowork 根据你给的所有反馈去更新这个技能，接着你还得知道去哪里读这个技能，确认反馈是不是按你想要的方式吸收进去了。把这个流程做得足够顺畅，让它做起来不痛苦，也是我们的责任。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Amazing. Is there anything else, Cat, you wanted to share? Anything else you wanted to leave listeners with? Anything you wanted to double down on that we haven't already touched on before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 太棒了。Cat，你还有什么想分享的吗？在进入我们激动人心的快问快答之前，有没有什么想留给听众的话，或者想再强调一下、我们还没聊到的内容？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I see a lot of people playing around with AI and building prototype apps and tinkering with building workflows. I would really push people towards building apps that you're actually using every single day because I think only through that usage are you actually getting the value. If you build a prototype app that isn't helping you get more done, then the AI isn't really adding value to your day.
turns.zh: 我看到很多人在玩 AI，做原型应用，捣鼓搭建各种工作流。我真心建议大家去做那种你自己每天都在用的应用，因为只有通过这样的使用，你才能真正获得价值。如果你做了一个原型应用，却没有帮你多做成任何事，那 AI 就没有真正给你的一天增加价值。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And there's only so much you learn from that when it's like, okay, I just did one-shotted something, oh, that's cool, and then you never come back to it. You're not learning a lot.
turns.zh: 而且从那种东西里能学到的也有限，就是「好，我一次性生成了个东西，哇，挺酷」，然后就再也不回头用它了。这样学不到多少东西。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: And you're not getting much leverage from it.
turns.zh: 而且你也没从中获得多少杠杆。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: And actual leverage. Yeah, that's such a good point.
turns.zh: 没错，真正的杠杆。这一点说得太好了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I also think there's a lot of people who spend a lot of time customizing their workflow. So I think there's two ends of the spectrum. One is people who never customize or never build automations, but there's this polar opposite end of people who obsess around customizing their tool, adding a ton of skills and MCPs and these workflow improvements, and I think sometimes that can even distract from your core goal of launching some product or building some feature. I think there's a lot of fun in customizing and we definitely want to make our products very hackable so that you can make it work really well for you, but there is a limit to how much it's useful, and I think there's a camp of people who maybe spend so much time customizing that they're not sleeping and not doing the core task that they originally set out to do.
turns.zh: 我还觉得，有很多人花大量时间去定制自己的工作流。我觉得这里有两个极端：一端是从不定制、从不搭建自动化的人，而另一端恰好相反，是那些痴迷于定制工具的人，加一大堆技能、MCP 和各种工作流改进。我觉得有时候这甚至会让你偏离核心目标，比如发布某个产品或做出某个功能。定制本身有很多乐趣，我们也确实希望让产品非常好改造，让你能把它调教得特别顺手，但它的用处是有上限的。我觉得有这么一群人，花了太多时间在定制上，以至于不睡觉，也没去做他们当初打算做的核心任务。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I see a lot of that on Twitter. Just like, "Look at my setup. It's out of control. It's so optimized," and what are you actually building? No, but my setup is so awesome. It gets so much done.
turns.zh: 我在推特上看到很多这种。就是「看我的配置，已经失控了，优化得太极致了」，那你到底在做什么东西呢？「不，可我的配置太棒了，效率特别高。」

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think the simple setups actually work better.
turns.zh: 我觉得简单的配置反而更好用。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: /powerup. Level up a little bit.
turns.zh: /powerup。稍微升个级。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah,
turns.zh: 对，

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Yeah. There's this Karpathy tweet that just came out yesterday where you talked about this divide that's interesting between people that tried ChatGPT, Claude back in the day, it was like, okay, and they're like, "Nah, this is terrible," and they kind of gave up on what AI could do for them and they're just so cynical of like, "No way, it's not actually that big of a deal." And then there's people that are using it to code essentially who see the full intense power of it and how good it is and people on both sides don't understand the other side and how they see the world. And so your advice is really good here to just actually use it for real things and see how good it actually has gotten.
turns.zh: 对。昨天刚出了一条 Karpathy 的推文，你也提到过这种有意思的分化：有些人在早些年试过 ChatGPT、Claude，觉得「嗯，这也太烂了」，就对 AI 能为自己做什么放弃了，非常愤世嫉俗，觉得「不可能，其实没那么了不起」。而另一边是那些用它写代码的人，他们看到了它的全部威力，知道它有多强，两边的人都无法理解对方，也不理解对方眼中的世界。所以你的建议在这里特别好：就是真的用它去做实事，看看它现在到底变得有多好。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah. I think the big shift is that the 2024 generation of products were chat-based and the Claude Code generation of products is action-based, and the big aha moment people have is when Claude can just do things on your behalf. It is an amazing feeling to know that the agent is capable of doing so much more than telling you what to do. The agent can actually just do it itself, and when people feel that, I think that's the eye-opening moment.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得最大的转变是，2024 年那一代产品是基于聊天的，而 Claude Code 这一代产品是基于行动的，人们最大的顿悟时刻，就是 Claude 能直接替你把事情做了。知道智能体能做的远不止告诉你该怎么做，它自己就能直接做，这种感觉太棒了，我觉得人们一旦有了这种感受，就是醍醐灌顶的时刻。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Shout out Chrome Extension, the Claude Code Chrome Extension, which you could just watch it doing stuff and you'd be like, "Fill out this form for me," and I'm like, "All right, here I go."
turns.zh: 给 Chrome 扩展点个赞，就是 Claude Code 的 Chrome 扩展，你可以看着它自己干活，你说「帮我填一下这个表单」，然后我就想，「好，来了」。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Exactly.
turns.zh: 没错。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Okay. Anything else before we get to our very exciting lightning round?
turns.zh: 好。在进入我们激动人心的快问快答之前，还有别的要说吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: No, let's do it.
turns.zh: 没了，开始吧。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Let's do it. Cat, I've got five questions for you. Welcome to the Lightning Round. There's this animation that plays, I have to make sure to say it. Are you ready?
turns.zh: 来吧。Cat，我有五个问题要问你。欢迎来到快问快答。这里会播一段动画，我得记得说一下。准备好了吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I'm ready.
turns.zh: 准备好了。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: First question, what are two or three books that you find yourself recommending most to other people?
turns.zh: 第一个问题，你最常向别人推荐的两三本书是什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I really like How Asia Works. It's a story about economic development and what are the policies and governments that make long-lasting successful economies. The other books that I'm really into are The Technology Trap. So this is actually about the past few technology revolutions, so the Industrial Revolution and the Computer Revolution and how this has affected workers. The reason that I really like this is because I think there's a lot we can learn from history to make sure that this transition goes well. And maybe on a fun note, I really like Paper Menagerie. It's just a book of short stories about coming of age and AI and just self-discovery.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢《亚洲是如何运转的》（How Asia Works）。它讲的是经济发展，以及什么样的政策和政府能造就长久成功的经济体。我另外很喜欢的一本是《技术陷阱》（The Technology Trap）。它其实讲的是过去几次技术革命，也就是工业革命和计算机革命，以及它们如何影响了劳动者。我喜欢它的原因是，我觉得我们可以从历史里学到很多东西，来确保这一次转型能够顺利。再说点轻松的，我很喜欢《纸动物园》（Paper Menagerie），那是一本短篇小说集，讲成长、AI，还有自我发现。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Favorite recent movie or TV show you have really enjoyed?
turns.zh: 最近有没有特别喜欢的电影或电视剧？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I really like Drive to Survive. There's no deeper meaning to it. There's just something very satisfying about people being so obsessed with a singular engineering goal and just the purity of the pursuit. And I also really love Free Solo, which is about Alex Honnold climbing El Capitan without a harness, and I think similarly, it's just such a pure achievement to be able to climb this extremely challenging, dangerous route and to be able to have the mental focus to do it knowing that if you make a single mistake, you die.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢《一级方程式：飞速人生》（Drive to Survive）。它没什么更深的意义，就是看到一群人对同一个工程目标如此痴迷，那种纯粹的追求让人特别满足。我也特别爱《徒手攀岩》（Free Solo），讲的是 Alex Honnold 不带任何保护绳攀登酋长岩。我觉得同样地，这是一种极其纯粹的成就：要爬一条极其困难又危险的路线，还要有足够的专注力，明知只要错一步就会丧命。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: It's insane. Yeah, that movie's out of control. And it's interesting how these relate in some way to the work you do.
turns.zh: 太疯狂了。对，那部电影简直离谱。而且有意思的是，它们在某种程度上和你做的工作有关联。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I actually am a rock climber, but I first watched Free Solo before I climbed rocks. And so I thought it was impressive, but I didn't understand how impressive it was. It's one of the rare movies where the more you know about it, the more you're blown away by how insane this is. The kinds of moves doing on the wall are things that I don't think I will ever be able to do in my lifetime if it were set in a gym one feet off the ground.
turns.zh: 其实我自己是攀岩的，但我是在开始攀岩之前看的《徒手攀岩》。所以当时我觉得很厉害，却不明白到底有多厉害。这是少有的那种电影：你越懂行，就越被它的疯狂震撼。他在岩壁上做的那些动作，就算放在离地一英尺的攀岩馆里，我这辈子也未必做得到。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: With a rope.
turns.zh: 还得带着绳子。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: With a rope.
turns.zh: 对，带着绳子。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Did you see the documentary in that other guy, the younger one that went on ice mountains?
turns.zh: 你看过另一个纪录片吗？讲另一个更年轻的人，去爬冰山的那个。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I did. That one was very sad.
turns.zh: 看过。那部很让人难过。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: But that was wild. Okay, favorite product you've recently discovered that you really love.
turns.zh: 但那部也很震撼。好，说说你最近发现的、特别喜欢的产品。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: The product that has most changed my life outside of Claude products is probably Waymo. I'm a diehard Waymo user, use it twice a day, get to and from work. So the two things that I really like about it are, one, I don't feel bad if a Waymo is waiting for me, and so I feel less pressure to be right at the curbside the moment it arrives, and the second thing is I feel like it lets me be a bit more productive. When I'm in the car with another human, I typically try not to do any work calls. I feel a little rude if I'm on my laptop the whole time. But one thing I really appreciate about the Waymo is I can call into a work call. I'm not worried about someone overhearing me. I'm not worried about, "Hey, is this rude? Am I talking too loud? Do I need to ask someone to change the music?" And so I feel like this has given me back 30 minutes every day.
turns.zh: 除了 Claude 的产品之外，最改变我生活的产品大概是 Waymo。我是 Waymo 的忠实用户，每天用两次，上下班都坐。我特别喜欢它的两点：第一，如果 Waymo 在等我，我不会有愧疚感，所以不用一到就非得立刻站在路边；第二，我觉得它让我能更高效一些。和另一个人同车时，我一般尽量不开工作电话，一直开着笔记本电脑也会觉得有点失礼。但 Waymo 的好处是我可以直接打进工作电话，不用担心被别人听到，也不用纠结「这样是不是不礼貌？我是不是说话太大声了？要不要请司机换首歌？」所以我觉得它每天帮我多出了 30 分钟。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: All these second order effects of technology, it's so interesting.
turns.zh: 技术带来的这些二阶效应，真的很有意思。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah. I always saw Waymo needed to be priced lower than Uber and Lyft to succeed, but actually I'm very happy to pay a 2X premium for it.
turns.zh: 是啊。我一直以为 Waymo 得比 Uber 和 Lyft 定价低才能成功，但其实我非常乐意为它多付两倍的价钱。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: I love Waymo. It's just like once you see it, you're just like, "This is insane." And then you get used to it. You get in there, you're like, "This is crazy," and then you forget about it.
turns.zh: 我爱 Waymo。就是那种，你第一次见到会觉得「这太疯狂了」，然后很快就习惯了。坐进去的时候你觉得「这也太神了」，然后你就把这事忘了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Totally. And I think it's also changed the vernacular. A lot of people at Anthropic love Waymo, and I think in the past you'd be like, "Hey, let's call our rideshare app," and now everyone's just like, "Okay, is Waymo here?"
turns.zh: 没错。我觉得它还改变了大家的用语。Anthropic 里很多人都爱 Waymo，以前你会说「嘿，我们叫一下打车软件吧」，现在大家都是「好，Waymo 到了吗？」

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Okay, two more questions. Do you have a favorite life motto that you often come back to in work or in life?
turns.zh: 好，还有两个问题。你有没有一句常常回想起的人生格言，不管是工作上还是生活中？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Just do things.
turns.zh: Just do things（去做就是了）。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: That tracks. That tracks.
turns.zh: 这很符合你。太符合了。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think there's a lot of value in first principles thinking, and if you know what you're optimizing for and you have strong first principles, then you can normally deduce what the right course of action is and be able to clearly articulate that to all the stakeholders, and then you should just do it. I think jobs are fake. If you understand the constraints, you can figure out what you can do and then just try to do it quickly, learn from the mistakes and apologize or fix them if you did something wrong.
turns.zh: 我觉得第一性原理思考很有价值：如果你清楚自己在优化什么，又有扎实的第一性原理，通常就能推导出正确的行动方向，也能向所有相关方讲清楚，然后就该去做了。我觉得职位这东西都是虚的。只要你理解约束条件，就能想清楚自己能做什么，然后尽快去做，从错误中学习，做错了就道歉或修正。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: You could just do things, whoever said that.
turns.zh: 你就是可以直接去做事，不管这话是谁说的。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think it's liberating actually to tell people this. I think in a lot of companies, roles are very strictly defined like, okay, this is what the PM does, is what the designer does, this is what an engineer does, and then even team scopes are very rigidly defined. So hey, this corner of the code base we touch and this corner, we're not allowed to touch, and I think what just do things lets people do is they feel empowered to make these decisions, empowered to operate across team boundaries just to get something done.
turns.zh: 其实我觉得把这话告诉大家是一种解放。在很多公司里，角色定义得非常死：这是 PM 做的，这是设计师做的，这是工程师做的，连团队范围也划得很僵，比如这块代码我们可以碰，那块我们不许碰。而我觉得「去做就是了」让人们感到被赋权，敢于做这些决定，敢于跨越团队边界把事情办成。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: That feels like a big important skill to be good at. People call it agency, just do the things they need to do.
turns.zh: 这感觉是一项很重要、值得练好的能力。大家管它叫主观能动性，就是主动去做该做的事。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Bias towards action.
turns.zh: 行动优先。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Bias towards action, all these ways of describing just don't wait for permission.
turns.zh: 行动优先，各种说法其实都是一个意思：别等着别人批准。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah. I think this is my favorite reason to work at a startup at some point in your life because one thing that was very life-changing for me was actually working at scale when we were 20 people, and so there was just no process and we had really big problems that we needed to solve. And I really appreciate Alex and the rest of the team for empowering me and the rest of the team to just figure things out without any boundaries for what sales supposed to do, what ops supposed to do, what engineer is supposed to do. Just like you have all the tools at your disposal, you have some ambitious hairy problem statement and you can do whatever you need to get to a good solution.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得这是人生中至少应该去一次创业公司的最好理由。对我来说，影响很大的一点是我在公司只有 20 个人的时候就经历过规模化，那时候没有任何流程，却有很大的问题要解决。我特别感谢 Alex 和团队其他人，让我和团队其他人可以自己摸索，没有任何边界，比如销售该干什么、运营该干什么、工程师该干什么。你手上有所有的工具，面前有一个雄心勃勃又棘手的问题，你可以不择手段地找到一个好的解法。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: You almost need that experience to build that skill to feel comfortable doing that because a lot of people, they go through school or in college and all these do the thing we tell you to do and then you will get a good grade, and you have to kind of unlearn that of like, okay, I'm just going to do the thing that needs to be done, and even if people think it's dumb, I think it's the right thing to do.
turns.zh: 你几乎需要这种经历才能培养出这项能力，才会觉得这样做心安理得。因为很多人在学校、大学里，一直是「照我们说的做，你就能拿好成绩」，你得把这套逻辑忘掉，变成「我就去做该做的事，哪怕别人觉得很蠢，我也认为这是对的」。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah, exactly.
turns.zh: 对，没错。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Okay. I actually have two more quick questions, two more final questions. One is when Claude thinks there's all these, I don't know if you call them verbs, what's the term for these things?
turns.zh: 好。我其实还有两个简短的问题，最后两个。第一个是，当 Claude 在思考的时候，会冒出各种词，我不知道你们管它们叫动词还是什么，这些东西叫什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Thinking words.
turns.zh: 思考词。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Thinking words. And interestingly, these all leaked in the source code. Do you have a favorite thinking word?
turns.zh: 思考词。有意思的是，这些词全都在源码泄露时被曝光了。你有最喜欢的思考词吗？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I really like manifesting. It's also like the sticker that I have on my laptop. It's my favorite.
turns.zh: 我很喜欢「manifesting」（显化）。它也是我笔记本电脑上贴的贴纸，是我的最爱。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Clearly the winner. Okay. Final question. Asked Forest this too, with AGI potentially arriving in our lifetime, when you don't potentially have to work, what are you going to do? What are you going to do with all your time?
turns.zh: 毫无悬念的赢家。好，最后一个问题。我也问过 Forest 这个问题：AGI 有可能在我们有生之年到来，当你不再需要工作的时候，你打算做什么？你会拿所有的时间去做什么？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: I think it will take a long time for AGI to diffuse across society. So I think the immediate thing is actually just helping bring the world along. I think my non-serious answer for it after this happens is I'll probably just do a lot of rock climbing. I'll probably just live in some... I'll probably move to Fontainebleau and just live amongst 10,000 boulders and climb for a bit. There's also so many books I want to read that... My goal is to be able to read one or two books a week, and I'm currently at probably 0.5. The backlog is pretty big. I think there's just so much we can learn from history and so much that I don't understand as well as I would love to. I don't know anything about physics or robotics or any hardware or aerospace or... There's just so many interesting topics. So I'm excited to learn, even knowing that the AGI will already know it.
turns.zh: 我觉得 AGI 要在社会中扩散开会花很长时间，所以眼下最要紧的其实是帮助世界跟上来。至于不太正经的回答，等那一天到来之后，我大概会去疯狂攀岩。我可能会搬到枫丹白露，住在一万块巨石中间，攀爬一阵子。还有很多书想读……我的目标是每周读一两本，而我现在大概只有 0.5 本，积压的书单相当长。我觉得从历史中可以学到太多东西，也有太多我理解得不够好、很想弄明白的东西。我对物理、机器人、任何硬件或航空航天之类的一无所知……有太多有趣的主题了。所以我很期待去学习，哪怕明知道 AGI 早就懂了。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Cat, this was amazing. You're awesome. Two follow-up questions. Where can folks find you online if they want to reach out and just follow what you're up to, and how can listeners be useful to you?
turns.zh: Cat，这期太棒了，你真了不起。还有两个后续问题：大家在网上哪里可以找到你，想联系你、关注你的动态的话？另外，听众怎样才能帮到你？

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: The best way to reach out is I am _catwu on Twitter. Feel free to tag me in things. Feel free to DM me. I read all my DMs. I don't always respond to every single one, but I will read them all. And then the thing that is most helpful is tell us where Claude Code and Cowork aren't working well for you. We are very grateful for the amount of positive feedback, but the thing that we thrive on is edge cases, errors, like specific tasks that we can reproduce where Claude Code or Cowork fail, because if you're able to share that with us and we're able to reproduce it, then this is something that we're able to actively improve for our next generations of models and for our next harnesses.
turns.zh: 联系我最好的方式是在 Twitter 上找 _catwu。欢迎在帖子里 @ 我，也欢迎私信我。我所有的私信都会看，虽然不一定每条都回，但我都会读。至于最有帮助的事，就是告诉我们 Claude Code 和 Cowork 在哪些地方对你不好用。我们非常感谢大家给的很多正面反馈，但我们真正靠它成长的是边缘情况、错误，也就是我们能复现的、Claude Code 或 Cowork 做不好的具体任务。因为如果你能分享给我们，我们也能复现，那我们就可以在下一代模型和下一代运行框架里主动去改进它。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Extremely cool. Everyone on... People on Twitter are not shy with sharing this feedback, so keep it going.
turns.zh: 太棒了。Twitter 上的朋友们分享反馈从来不害羞，所以继续保持。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yes, please share the problems that you're having with us.
turns.zh: 对，请把你们遇到的问题分享给我们。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Yeah, and it's really cool to see all your team being so active on Twitter and responding to people. And so what I'm hearing, this is actually stuff you guys actually see and react to.
turns.zh: 对，而且看到你们整个团队在 Twitter 上这么活跃、积极回复大家，真的很棒。所以我听到的是，你们确实会看到这些内容并做出回应。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Yeah. We appreciate everyone being so engaged with us. It gives a team a ton of energy. We have this channel of user love, and so whenever you guys share a success story, we post it there and whenever you guys share issues with our product, we put it into our feedback channel, that way our broader team is able to act on it.
turns.zh: 是的。我们感谢大家这么积极地和我们互动，这给团队带来了很大的能量。我们有一个「用户喜爱」频道，大家分享成功故事时，我们就发到那里；大家反馈产品问题时，我们就放进反馈频道，这样我们更广泛的团队就能据此行动。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: That is so cool to know. Thanks for sharing that. Well, Cat, thank you so much for being here.
turns.zh: 知道这些太好了，谢谢分享。好，Cat，非常感谢你来做客。

turns.speaker: guest
turns.text: Thanks for having me.
turns.zh: 谢谢你邀请我。

turns.speaker: host
turns.text: Bye, everyone.
turns.zh: 大家再见。
